title: The divisible pool shrank from 89 to 74-80 per cent of gross tax revenue while the states' share of it rose from 32 to 41
summary: Article 270(1) shares "all taxes and duties referred to in the Union List" with the states except the surcharges of Article 271 and any cess levied "for the purposes of the Union". Over the period of this instrument the Union's use of that exception grew: the divisible pool fell from 89.1 per cent of gross tax revenue in FY2014-15 to a 74.0-79.9 per cent band across FY2020-21 to FY2023-24, and cesses and surcharges rose from 10.4 per cent of gross tax revenue in FY2011-12 to between 15.3 and 20.2 per cent by the end of the decade depending on the convention used. The states' recommended share of the pool rose from 32 to 42 to 41 per cent over the same period. The two movements run in opposite directions and both are real. BOTH COMPARISONS IN THAT SENTENCE CROSS DECLARED BREAKS AND THE FIGURES ARE NOT ON ONE BASIS. FY2014-15 sits before the Fourteenth Finance Commission award boundary and FY2020-21 to FY2023-24 sit inside the Fifteenth, and every quantity keyed to an award changes at that boundary (P-103); the cess and surcharge shares also mix Actuals, Revised Estimates and Budget Estimates inside published series, including in the publications of the bodies that produce them (P-113). The direction is robust to both — the divisible pool fell and cesses rose on any basis — but the SIZE of the fall is a comparison across two seams and should not be read as one measured change.
whatHappened: The Sixteenth Finance Commission put both ends of the movement in one sentence at para 7.67: "With cesses and surcharges having cut the size of the divisible pool from 89.1 per cent of GTR in 2014-15 to a 74-80 per cent range during the first four years of the FC-15 award period for which actuals are available, there is no room for cutting the States' share in it." The Union's own accounts make the mechanism visible at the level of a single tax head: of gross Union excise duty of ₹3,05,362.18 crore in FY2023-24, the CAG certified ₹33,820.71 crore as entering the divisible pool — 11.1 per cent. Gross basic excise duty that year was ₹33,786.92 crore, so the certified net proceeds of Union excise duty are, to within ₹34 crore, the basic duty and nothing else. That ratio is fully supported by published Union sources and is stated by none of them.
assessmentNote: No objective was stated at announcement because there was no announcement: no Union measure was ever presented as shrinking the divisible pool. Each levy was introduced on its own stated purpose and the aggregate effect is a residual nobody claimed. The value asserts nothing about the finding's quality — the arithmetic is certified for one year and reconciles to the second decimal.
caseFor: Articles 270 and 271 place cesses and surcharges outside the shareable pool by design, and the design is older than this government: the Constitution has read this way since 1950, and the Union has told Parliament in terms that the Article exempts cesses and surcharges from distribution and that they therefore do not form part of the divisible pool. A cess is money raised for a named national purpose — health, education, roads, agricultural infrastructure, disaster response — and those purposes are national precisely because no single state will fund them at the level the country needs. The Union also carries the whole of defence, external affairs, interest on the national debt and the countercyclical burden in a downturn, none of which is shared. Against that, the states have had the largest single-step devolution increase in the institution's history: tax devolution rose from an FC-XIII average of 27.9 per cent of gross tax revenue to 34.0 per cent under FC-XIV and 32.1 per cent under FC-XV, levels never reached before 2015. And the Sixteenth Finance Commission, having examined the states' complaint about cesses in full, declined either to cap them or to bring them into the pool.
caseAgainst: The states' case does not require the exception to be unconstitutional; it requires only that its size be measured, and the measurement is the Union's own. A rise of roughly ten points in the non-shareable share is not a rounding of the constitutional design but a re-proportioning of it, achieved without any vote in which the states could participate. The Fourteenth Finance Commission conceded the point in terms — the first of its four reasons for going to 42 per cent was "States not being entitled to the growing share of cess and surcharges in the revenues of the Union Government" — which means the headline increase the Union cites was itself partly compensation for this, and the trend continued afterwards. The Union excise arithmetic is the sharpest form: 88.9 per cent of a Union tax sat outside the pool in FY2023-24 and no published document says so. And the states have no instrument at all: they do not administer Union cesses, have no assessment machinery for them, and every figure they can put before a Commission is a Union figure.
differentFactsNote: A weighting case, not a different-facts case, and the distinction matters because the surface suggests otherwise. Both sides use the same published series — the Commission's divisible-pool share and the Union's own Receipt Budget line items — and neither contradicts the other's arithmetic. What they disagree about is whether a constitutionally permitted exception growing from a tenth to a fifth of gross tax revenue is the design working or the design being used up. A single ledger placing both facts side by side exists and is built here: divisible-pool-share-gtr against fc-vertical-devolution-share.

unmeasured.what: A definition of "cesses and surcharges" as an aggregate
unmeasured.why: No Indian statute, budget document or Finance Commission report defines the set. Article 270(1) excludes cesses and surcharges but supplies no list and no test, and the Receipt Budget carries no total line — the aggregate can only be computed by a reader selecting line items, which is why four published sources give four different sums for the same year.

unmeasured.what: The bridge between the Receipt Budget's gross tax revenue and the CAG's certified net proceeds
unmeasured.why: Annex 4C gives the destination and the tax-revenue statement gives the origin; nothing published gives the road between them. Union excise reconciles to about ₹5 crore in 34 lakh and corporation tax to about ₹1,122 crore, but customs does not reconcile at all: ₹32,136.74 crore, 13.8 per cent of the head, is unexplained, and at the whole-tax-revenue level the residual is 1.27 percentage points of gross tax revenue, about ₹44,000 crore.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A head-by-head reconciliation published alongside Annex 4C, or the CAG certificate itself with its workings.

unmeasured.what: Any state-side measurement of Union cess collections
unmeasured.why: The states do not administer Union cesses and have no assessment machinery for them, so no state figure exists or can exist. This phase's usual pairing — the Union's figure against the state's figure, both quoted, neither adopted — is structurally unavailable for its central quantity.

title: The Fourteenth Finance Commission raises the states' share of the divisible pool from 32 to 42 per cent
summary: The Fourteenth Finance Commission, chaired by Y.V. Reddy, reported on 15 December 2014 and recommended that the states' share of the divisible pool rise from 32 to 42 per cent with effect from FY2015-16 — the largest single-step increase in the history of the institution and the first departure from the incremental 1.5-point moves of the Eleventh, Twelfth and Thirteenth Commissions. The Union accepted it in full.
claimAtLaunch: FC-XIV para 8.13, verbatim: "increasing the share of tax devolution to 42 per cent of the divisible pool", on four stated considerations — "(i) States not being entitled to the growing share of cess and surcharges in the revenues of the Union Government; (ii) the importance of increasing the share of tax devolution in total transfers; (iii) an aggregate view of the revenue expenditure needs of States without Plan and non-Plan distinction; and (iv) the space available with the Union Government." The same paragraph states the intended character of the move: "a compositional shift in transfers from grants to tax devolution... it does not impose an additional fiscal burden on the Union Government."
whatHappened: The share moved to 42 per cent and stayed there for the whole award. Devolution rose from 27.1 per cent of the Union's gross tax revenue in FY2014-15 to an FC-XIV award average of 34.0 per cent, and in rupees from ₹3,37,835 crore to ₹5,06,191 crore in the first year alone. Finance Commission grants as a share of gross tax revenue moved 5.1 to 5.8 in the same year and averaged 5.4 across the award against 4.6 under FC-XIII, so the promised compositional shift toward devolution happened without the grant channel collapsing. What also happened over the same five years is that the pool the 42 per cent applied to fell from 89.1 to 80.9 per cent of gross tax revenue.
assessmentNote:
INDEPENDENCE, RESTATED AFTER THE 2026-08-06 PASS: this is the one record in the class that survives every test. The evidence is intra-state — a later Finance Commission reporting on an earlier one — and it QUALIFIES under the intra-state test because a Commission report is that Commission’s own constitutional function, not a document produced in support of the claim; Table 7.5 and Annexure 7.1 are the Sixteenth Commission’s own computation and Figure 7.4 states CAG certificates as its source on the face of the figure. No limb of the recommendation is unmeasured. A reader should still know what kind of evidence this is: one arm of the state measuring another, which is better than a body scoring itself and is not the same as a source outside the state.

PREVIOUS NOTE, PRESERVED VERBATIM: The value scores the recommendation against the objective stated at announcement, which was to raise the states' share of the divisible pool to 42 per cent. That was recommended, accepted and paid. It does NOT score the net position of the states, which depends on the size of the pool and belongs to L-0150. Reading this record alone as "devolution rose sharply" is the error the pairing of the two records exists to prevent.
caseFor: Neither the number nor the acceptance is in dispute. A Commission constituted under Article 280 recommended the largest increase ever made, the Union accepted it without modification and paid it for five years, and the states' share of gross tax revenue rose by about seven percentage points. The Commission expressly rejected a minimum guaranteed devolution at para 8.14, so what the states received was a share of whatever the pool turned out to be, and they received it untied — money a state legislature appropriates rather than money a Union ministry conditions. On the Union's own framing the shift was fiscally neutral to it, achieved by converting grants into devolution, which is a transfer of discretion to the states at no cost to them.
caseAgainst: The Commission's own first reason for the increase was that the states were not entitled to the growing share of cesses and surcharges — so the headline gain was, on the umpire's own account, partly compensation for a loss the states were already sustaining, and the loss continued afterwards. Against a rise of ten points in the share, the pool fell about eight points over the same award and a further seven by FY2020-21. A share of a shrinking base is not the same instrument as a share of a stable one, and the Commission did not fix the base. The compositional shift also carried a cost the paragraph does not mention: converting grants to devolution moved money out of formulae that could be targeted at need and into a formula fixed for five years, which is why the Commission's successors first rebuilt the grant channel and then dismantled it again.
differentFactsNote: Both sides accept the recommendation, the acceptance, the rupee figures and the pool arithmetic. The disagreement is about which denominator the 42 per cent should be read against, and that is a weighting of one agreed ledger, not two ledgers.

title: 42 becomes 41: Jammu and Kashmir leaves the denominator, and the one per cent retained has no ledger
summary: The states' share of the divisible pool moved from 42 to 41 per cent with effect from FY2020-21. It is not a cut. The Fifteenth Finance Commission reduced the share by approximately the erstwhile State of Jammu and Kashmir's own entitlement, because J&K had ceased to be a state, leaving the twenty-eight remaining states with a broadly equivalent amount. The one per cent so retained has no published account of any kind.
whatHappened: FC-XV para 6.9, verbatim: the Commission "only adjusted for the newly carved out Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, keeping the balance share broadly equivalent at 41 per cent for the remaining twenty-eight States." FC-XVI para 7.16 puts a number on it: the erstwhile state's share was estimated at "approximately 1 per cent of the divisible pool." The Union's own Explanatory Memorandum of 1 February 2021 frames the same fact a third way, as money "retained with the Central Government for financing the requirements of the newly formed Union Territories". J&K's inter-se share across FC-XI to FC-XV runs 1.29, 1.30, 1.55, 1.85, 0.00.
assessmentNote: Contested rather than no-objective because a claim was made and its outcome is unmeasured: the Union stated that the retained share finances the requirements of the new Union Territories, and no instrument tracks whether it did. Where a claim exists and its outcome is unmeasured the value is contested, not no-objective.
caseFor: The arithmetic is the Commission's, is stated in terms, and is correct: a state that no longer exists cannot hold an inter-se share, and leaving 42 per cent in place would have handed J&K's entitlement to the other twenty-eight states as a windfall. The Union does not merely retain the one per cent — it now carries the entire expenditure of two Union Territories that were previously a state financing itself out of its own share, and the J&K panchayat grants already in this instrument show money reaching the territory. Every published account of the step, by the Commission, by its successor and by the Union, describes the same movement.
caseAgainst: Three institutions give three descriptions of one transaction and none of them is a reconciliation. The Commission says it kept the states "broadly equivalent"; the successor Commission says the adjustment was "approximately 1 per cent"; the Union says the money is "retained with the Central Government" for the Union Territories' requirements. "Broadly" and "approximately" are the load-bearing words and neither is quantified. More consequentially, nothing published sets the retained share against expenditure in the two Union Territories: there is no annual statement, no identified head of account and no audit of it, so a sum of roughly a percentage point of the divisible pool passed out of a formula into general Union revenue with no ledger following it. The change is also permanent in a way its reason is not: if J&K becomes a state again the 41 does not revert of itself.
differentFactsNote: Both sides accept the constitutional fact, the arithmetic and the three published framings. The disagreement is whether an unreconciled residue of that size is acceptable without an account, which is a weighting of one agreed record.

unmeasured.what: What became of the approximately one per cent of the divisible pool retained on Jammu and Kashmir's reorganisation
unmeasured.why: No published instrument states the amount in rupees for any year, identifies a head of account for it, or sets it against expenditure in the two Union Territories. Three institutions describe the movement and none reconciles it.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A statement in the Union Receipt Budget or Expenditure Profile identifying the retained share and its application, or an Article 279 certificate distinguishing it.

unmeasured.what: Any written derivation of the "approximately 1 per cent" adjustment
unmeasured.why: The finding is that a one percentage point cut to the divisible pool was applied with no written derivation anywhere. Neither Commission publishes a calculation, and the arithmetic does not close: J&K's FC-XIV inter-se share of 1.854 per cent of the states' 42 per cent is 0.78 per cent of the pool, not 1 per cent, and no document states whether the Ladakh component, population updating or the service-tax carve-out accounts for the difference. Graded not-collected rather than not-published because if no derivation was ever committed to paper there is nothing a compulsion could produce; the absence is of the working, not of its release. Re-graded on 2026-08-04.

title: The Sixteenth Finance Commission recommends nil revenue deficit, sector-specific and state-specific grants, and the Union takes note
summary: The Sixteenth Finance Commission reported on 17 November 2025 for the award period FY2026-27 to FY2030-31. It retained the vertical share at 41 per cent and recommended zero post-devolution revenue deficit grants, zero sector-specific grants and zero state-specific grants — three categories carrying ₹4,74,100 crore under its predecessor. Local body grants roughly double to ₹7,91,493 crore, with a ₹10,000 crore urbanisation premium and a ₹56,100 crore special infrastructure component. The Union accepted the vertical share, the horizontal shares, the local body grants and the disaster grants on 1 February 2026; on the assessment of state finances that produced the nil recommendation it recorded only that "The Government takes note of the above assessment."
claimAtLaunch: That state finances no longer require deficit financing through grants and that untied local body money is a better instrument than tied sectoral grants. The Commission's stated reason for retaining 41 per cent is the size of the pool: "With cesses and surcharges having cut the size of the divisible pool from 89.1 per cent of GTR in 2014-15 to a 74-80 per cent range... there is no room for cutting the States' share in it."
assessmentNote: The award commenced on 1 April 2026 and is four months old at the date of this record. The obstacle is elapsed time and the evidence time accumulates — whether the seventeen states that received revenue deficit grants under FC-XV can carry the loss, and whether doubled local body grants are actually released, are questions only years of releases answer. Not awaiting-adjudication: nothing is pending before any body outside the enacting authority.
caseFor: Revenue deficit grants were always a bridge and were designed to taper — seventeen states in FC-XV's first year falling to six by its last. A Commission that finds the bridge no longer needed and says so is doing its constitutional job, and the money did not vanish: the local body grant roughly doubles, moving it from state treasuries to the third tier, and an urbanisation premium responds to the one demographic fact every state agrees on. On sector-specific and state-specific grants the Commission was ratifying reality — its own audit found the Union had "largely discontinued releasing" both after FC-XIV and that nil of FC-XV's ₹49,599 crore of state-specific grants was ever released, so recommending them again would have recommended a fiction.
caseAgainst: The break at FY2025-26/FY2026-27 is total rather than incremental: two of six grant categories go to zero and the revenue-deficit-grant series simply ends. For the states that had them the loss is immediate and is not offset by the local body increase, which goes to panchayats and municipalities rather than to the state budget. The Commission reached its nil recommendation on an assessment of state finances, and the Union's response to that assessment was "takes note" — the weakest of its five undefined action verbs, so the Union has neither accepted nor rejected the reasoning while accepting the result that suits it. And the same Commission that found no room to cut the states' share of the pool declined to cap or bring in the cesses that shrank it, so the only instrument it used against the trend was one it had already ruled out changing.
differentFactsNote: Both sides accept the recommendation, the acceptance, the category totals and the Union's verb. The disagreement is whether abolishing a grant that was mostly not being paid is a reform or a ratification, and both readings rest on the same audit finding.

title: The Union's five action verbs under Article 281 have no definitions, and "due consideration" produced nil of ₹49,599 crore
summary: Article 281 requires the President to lay every Finance Commission recommendation before Parliament with an explanatory memorandum on the action taken. The Union's memoranda use a graded scale of verbs — accepted, accepted in-principle, due consideration will be given, takes note, will examine — and nothing anywhere defines any of them. On the Fifteenth Finance Commission's final report the Union accepted the vertical share, the revenue deficit grants, the local body grants and the disaster grants, and gave "due consideration" to ₹1,29,987 crore of sector-specific and ₹49,599 crore of state-specific grants. On 18 August 2025 the Ministry of Finance told the Lok Sabha, in terms, that "No State-specific grants were specifically accepted in the Explanatory Memorandum... Accordingly, no state-specific grants under 15th FC recommendations are being released."
whatHappened: The construction of one verb is now on the parliamentary record: "due consideration will be given" was construed by the Union, four and a half years later, as non-acceptance. Nil of ₹49,599 crore was released. The Sixteenth Finance Commission states as a finding of fact that the Union "largely discontinued releasing" sector- and state-specific grants after FC-XIV, and narrowed its own inquiry because of it. The scale continues: on FC-XVI's recommendations the Union in February 2026 accepted four blocks, accepted the borrowing ceilings in-principle, took note of the state-finance assessment, and said it would examine centrally sponsored scheme rationalisation, the power sector, subsidies and public-enterprise reform.
assessmentNote: The record finds something real and firmly established — a graded vocabulary with no definitions, one term of which has now been construed on the record as refusal — and no objective was stated at announcement against which it could be scored. The Union never claimed the verbs meant anything in particular; that is the finding. Not contested: no competing reading of the evidence exists, only a competing view of whether the practice is a defect.
caseFor: Article 281 requires the Union to lay an explanatory memorandum, not to accept anything. The Finance Commission is advisory on Article 275 grants and the Constitution deliberately leaves the Union free to decline; a memorandum saying "rejected" in plain terms would be constitutionally identical and politically worse, and the Union's answer to Parliament shows the position was stated when asked. The sector-specific grants were, on the Union's own account, folded into existing and new centrally sponsored and central sector schemes — the memorandum says so — so the money question and the label question are different questions. A body that reserves its position on twelve blocks while accepting nine is engaging with the report, not evading it.
caseAgainst: A vocabulary of five terms with no definitions is not a scale but a discretion described in the language of agreement. The states, the Commission and Parliament all read "due consideration will be given" in February 2021 as something other than refusal, and the Union's own later answer confirms it meant refusal from the start — a construction that could not be tested for four and a half years because nothing defined the term. The consequence is measurable: nil of ₹49,599 crore. The Sixteenth Finance Commission's response was to narrow its own inquiry, which is the clearest evidence that the practice changes what the constitutional umpire is willing to recommend. And the Union's own aggregate for FC-XV grants-in-aid differs from the Commission's by about ₹1.88 lakh crore — close to the ₹1,79,586 crore it declined — so the declined money was silently removed from the denominator of the Union's own performance statistic.
differentFactsNote: Every fact is agreed: the verbs, the amounts, the nil release and the parliamentary answer. The disagreement is whether an undefined vocabulary in a constitutionally mandated document is a defect or a permitted flexibility.

unmeasured.what: Definitions of the Union's five action verbs under Article 281
unmeasured.why: No statute, rule, manual or memorandum defines "accepted", "accepted in-principle", "due consideration will be given", "takes note" or "will examine", or states what follows from each. The scale is inferred from usage, and one term has been construed only retrospectively, in answer to a parliamentary question.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Ministry of Finance instruction, or a parliamentary answer stating the consequences of each verb.

unmeasured.what: Whether any of the ₹1,29,987 crore of unaccepted sector-specific grants was in fact released
unmeasured.why: The Union states the sectors would be given due consideration "while formulating and implementing existing and new Centrally Sponsored and Central Sector Schemes", which makes the money untraceable as Finance Commission grant. The state-specific half is resolved at nil; the sector-specific half is not.
unmeasured.wouldFill: The Demands for Grants for Transfers to States with scheme-level Actuals, or a parliamentary answer on the sector-specific head.

title: The certificate the Constitution makes final has been produced for seventy-six years and published once
summary: Article 279(1) provides that the net proceeds of any tax shall be ascertained and certified by the Comptroller and Auditor General, "whose certificate shall be final". That certificate fixes the divisible pool and therefore fixes, to the rupee, what every state is owed. It has never been published as a document of the Comptroller and Auditor General for any year. On the Sixteenth Finance Commission's recommendation, accepted by the Union, the Receipt Budget 2026-2027 carried Annex 4C for the first time — a disclosure statement of certified net proceeds for FY2023-24, published by the paying party.
claimAtLaunch: FC-XVI recommendation 2 (para 7.30), that the Union publish the CAG's Article 279 net-proceeds certificate annually; recorded as "accepted" in the Explanatory Memorandum of 1 February 2026.
whatHappened: Annex 4C gives certified net proceeds for FY2023-24 of ₹27,69,957.40 crore, itemised by tax head, with the states' share at 41 per cent of ₹11,35,682.53 crore against releases of ₹11,36,306.00 crore and a final settlement of minus ₹623.47 crore. Integrated GST and the GST Compensation Cess are named as lines and valued at a dash. Five earlier years reach the public record only through FC-XVI Table 7.4, sourced by the Commission to "CAG certificate". A sweep of the CAG's own audit-report index with a positive control returns no document containing "net proceeds", and the Regulations on Audit and Accounts 2020 contain zero occurrences of "net proceeds", "proceeds" or "279" — Regulation 43(1) provides only that the CAG certifies the Finance Accounts and the Appropriation Accounts. The CAG's own Union Government Finance Accounts reports carry a footnote reserving the certificate: "subject to final ascertainment and certification under Article 279(1)."
assessmentNote: The measure is the recommendation of annual publication, accepted and in force, and one year has been published. Whether the disclosure is annual is a question only elapsed time answers. Not awaiting-adjudication: nothing is pending before a body outside the enacting authority. Not partly: the objective was annual publication, and a single instance is not a partial series but the first term of one.
caseFor: The disclosure exists, is complete for the year it covers, and was made voluntarily on a recommendation the Union could have declined as it declined others. Nothing was hidden before: the operative constitutional fact is the settlement, and every rupee of devolution has been in the Receipt Budget and the Finance Accounts, audited annually, throughout. Article 279 makes the certificate final between the parties; it does not require publication, and the framers who wrote finality into the clause wrote no publication duty beside it. The Union has now supplied one anyway, and the first year's figure reconciles against its own gross tax revenue statement to the second decimal.
caseAgainst: A number the Constitution declares final, which determines what twenty-eight states are owed, was produced for seventy-six years without anyone outside the two parties seeing it. No regulation of the auditor governs it, so its form, timing and content rest on nothing published at all. What now exists is a disclosure by the payer of what the auditor certified — not the certificate — for one year, and the only other five years in the public record reach it through a Commission the payer appoints. The consequence is concrete: the series on which the entire cess argument turns has an independently certified basis for six years out of sixteen, and the states have never held a document with which to check the arithmetic of their own entitlement.
differentFactsNote: Both sides accept that the certificate exists, that it is final, that it was not published, and that one year now is. The disagreement is whether finality between two parties can be sound without disclosure to the party with less information, which is a weighting of an agreed record.

The Regulations on Audit and Accounts 2020 contain no provision for it. Its only published form is a disclosure statement in the Union's own Receipt Budget, for one year.

Extending Annexure 4C backwards over the years the certificate has already been issued would fill this, and needs no new computation - the certificates exist and have existed since 1950.

title: Cess proceeds are not credited to the funds the cesses were levied for, in ten consecutive audit reports
summary: A cess sits outside the divisible pool because it is levied for a stated purpose. In every Union Government financial audit report from FY2015-16 to FY2024-25 the Comptroller and Auditor General finds that large parts of cess collections were retained in the Consolidated Fund of India rather than credited to the reserve funds created for those purposes. The finding is not an incident: it recurs across ten reports, names different cesses in each, was accepted by the Ministry once and corrected once, and continues.
claimAtLaunch: Each levy's own enacting provision states the purpose for which it is imposed, and the Article 270(1) proviso puts a cess outside the shareable pool only because it is levied "for the purposes of the Union" — the purpose is the constitutional justification for the exclusion.
whatHappened: FY2018-19: 35 cesses, ₹2,74,592 crore collected against ₹1,64,322 crore transferred, with the GST Compensation Cess short-credited by ₹47,272 crore — accepted by the Ministry in February 2020 and corrected in FY2019-20. FY2021-22: ₹4,78,680 crore, 26.43 per cent of net tax receipts, with the Ministry's "over a period of years" defence recorded verbatim and the auditor's rejoinder beside it. FY2022-23: four funds, ₹2,41,220.26 crore collected against ₹344.48 crore transferred, with "Fund not created as yet" recorded against the Oil Industry Development Fund and against the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Fund, which had ₹1,51,092.71 crore accumulated. FY2023-24: ₹3,79,598 crore, 10.95 per cent of gross tax revenue, short transfer ₹3,69,307 crore; the Health and Education Cess apportionment shows nil to two of its three designated funds for four and five years running; and the Ministry of Finance's own cumulative transfer figure of ₹3,66,152.31 crore stands against the Union Government Finance Accounts' ₹2,64,632.07 crore, a gap of ₹1,01,520.24 crore which the auditor says "needs to be reconciled by the Ministry". FY2024-25: ₹3,89,220 crore, 10.25 per cent of gross tax revenue; the crude-oil cess has raised ₹3,12,782 crore since FY1974-75 with ₹2,94,150 crore still in the Consolidated Fund, and the Oil Industry Development Fund was operationalised for the first time.
assessmentNote: Failed against the objective stated in each levy's own enacting provision — that the proceeds finance the named purpose — which is also the constitutional ground on which the levy sits outside the divisible pool. The mechanism is non-transfer established by the auditor and accepted once by the Ministry, not a court striking anything down. The value does not assert that money was misspent: money in the Consolidated Fund is appropriated by Parliament, and the case for turns on exactly that.
caseFor: Money in the Consolidated Fund of India is neither lost nor diverted; it is subject to parliamentary appropriation, which is a stronger control than a reserve fund in the Public Account, and the expenditure the cess was meant to fund is in most cases made from the Consolidated Fund anyway. The Ministry's stated position, recorded by the auditor in FY2021-22, is that transfers are made over a period of years rather than in the year of collection, and the record supports it in part: the ₹47,272 crore GST compensation short-crediting was accepted and corrected the following year, and the Oil Industry Development Fund was created and operationalised in FY2024-25 after the auditor named it. A reserve fund is an accounting mechanism, not a spending guarantee, and creating one before the expenditure programme exists parks money rather than using it.
caseAgainst: The purpose is not decoration; it is the reason the money is outside the divisible pool at all. Every rupee retained in the Consolidated Fund against a designated fund is a rupee the states did not share, held for a purpose that did not receive it. The scale is the auditor's own: a short transfer of ₹3,69,307 crore in one year, a fund uncreated while ₹1,51,092.71 crore accumulated against it, nil to the Madhyamik and Uchchtar Shiksha Kosh for four consecutive years, and ₹2,94,150 crore of crude-oil cess still in the Consolidated Fund after half a century. The "over a period of years" defence was put to the auditor and rejected in the same paragraph. And the Union's own two statements of one quantity differ by ₹1.02 lakh crore with no reconciliation, which is evidence about the reliability of Union-origin figures generally — and every quantity in this dispute is a Union-origin figure.
differentFactsNote: The rupees are the auditor's and neither side disputes them; the Ministry's own defence concedes the timing and disputes only its significance. This is one ledger read two ways, which is what makes it a weighting case rather than a different-facts one.

title: The Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess: revenue-neutral at the pump, shareable revenue moved out of the pool, nil to its own fund for two years
summary: The Finance Bill 2021 imposed an Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess of ₹2.50 a litre on petrol and ₹4.00 a litre on high speed diesel with effect from 2 February 2021, and simultaneously cut basic excise duty and special additional excise duty so that the pump price barely moved. Basic excise duty is shareable with the states; the cess is not. The Union stated the revenue-neutrality of the package in four separate documents and did not mention the divisible pool in any of them. In the cess's first two full years, not one rupee was transferred to the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Fund it was created to finance.
claimAtLaunch: Four formulations in the Union's own documents: the Budget Speech at para 188 ("not to put additional burden on consumers on most items"); the Annexure to Part B at para 5 ("so that overall consumer does not bear any additional burden"); the Memorandum's section on the cess; and the Tax Research Unit's covering letter ("calibrated so that there would be no additional burden on the consumer"). The levying clauses open with the Article 270(1)-proviso formula: "There shall be levied and collected... for the purposes of the Union".
whatHappened: The consumer-neutrality objective was achieved almost exactly on three grades of four: reading the Union's own after-table against the rates its own amending notifications had left in force, the total per-litre levy on unbranded petrol moved 32.98 to 32.90 and on unbranded diesel 31.83 to 31.80 — minus eight paise and minus three paise. The composition changed: basic excise duty on unbranded petrol fell 2.98 to 1.40 and on unbranded diesel 4.83 to 1.80, a movement of ₹1.58 and ₹3.03 a litre out of the shareable pool. The Union's own Receipt Budget note 6.05 confirms that the special additional excise duty, also cut, is itself "commonly known as surcharge", so the shareable component of the movement is the basic-duty cut alone. The second objective failed for two years: the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Fund received nil, and the CAG recorded "Fund not created as yet" against it for FY2022-23 with ₹1,51,092.71 crore accumulated. The precedent is exact: the Finance Act 2018 introduced an ₹8-a-litre Road and Infrastructure Cess and cut basic excise duty and the road cess by exactly ₹8, migrating ₹2 a litre from the shareable side at nil cost to the consumer. The arithmetic now reconciles to the paisa with no rounding slack, from primary sources at both ends: 2.98 minus 1.40 is 1.58 and 4.83 minus 1.80 is 3.03, and the leg-sum identity (change in basic duty, plus change in special additional duty, plus the cess, equals the change in the total) holds on all four grades. The fourth grade is where the stated claim fails: branded diesel moved 34.19 to 34.20, one paisa dearer, which is recorded at L-0180. The 2018 precedent is confirmed from both ends, and the correct citations are the enacted sections — section 110 of the Finance Act 2018 for the Social Welfare Surcharge, 111 and 112 for the Road and Infrastructure Cess on imported and on excisable goods — fixed not by assumption but by notification 01/2021-Central Excise, which defines appropriate duties of excise on petrol to include the additional duty leviable under section 112 of the Finance Act 2018.
assessmentNote: Partly, on two stated objectives with opposite outcomes: consumer neutrality was achieved to within eight paise a litre, and the financing of agricultural infrastructure through the designated fund received nothing for two years. The value scores the stated objectives. The effect on the divisible pool is not scored here because no objective was stated for it, and that silence is recorded as an absence instead.
caseFor: Every element of the package is a power the Constitution confers and Parliament exercised: Article 271 for surcharges, the Article 270(1) proviso for cesses, and an ordinary Finance Bill to set rates. The stated purpose was to fund agricultural infrastructure without raising the pump price, and the rate table did exactly that, to within a few paise, in the middle of a farm-policy crisis. The revenue did not disappear: agricultural infrastructure spending is made from the Consolidated Fund under parliamentary appropriation, and a reserve fund created before the expenditure programme exists parks money rather than deploying it. The 2018 precedent shows the mechanism is not novel and was used in the open, with the full rate table printed in a Budget Speech annexure.
caseAgainst: The package is revenue-neutral to the consumer and is not revenue-neutral to the states, and the Union's own documents say the first and never mention the second. "Divisible pool", "devolution", "States' share" and "shareable" appear zero times across the Budget Speech Part B and its annexures, the Memorandum's cess sections and the Tax Research Unit letter. A measure whose entire fiscal content is the migration of revenue from a shared head to an unshared one was announced without the word "shared" appearing. And the purpose that justifies the exclusion received nil for two years while the cess raised over ₹1.5 lakh crore — so for two years the levy was neither shared nor applied to the purpose that exempted it from sharing.
differentFactsNote: The rate tables, the neutrality statements, the collections and the nil transfers are all the Union's own and none is disputed. The disagreement is whether an unmentioned distributional consequence is a defect in the announcement or simply not part of it.

title: The GST compensation guarantee: 14 per cent on a 2015-16 base, 1 July 2017 to 30 June 2022
summary: Section 18 of the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act 2016 commanded Parliament to compensate the states for revenue loss arising on account of the implementation of GST "for a period of five years". The GST (Compensation to States) Act 2017 gave every state a protected revenue growing at 14 per cent per annum compounded from a FY2015-16 base, compensation equal to protected revenue minus actual revenue, payable bi-monthly, funded by a compensation cess on demerit and luxury goods paid into a GST Compensation Fund, for a transition period ending 30 June 2022. The guarantee ran its full statutory life and expired by effluxion of time.
claimAtLaunch: To hold states harmless against revenue loss from the change of tax regime for five years. The Council's Chairperson characterised it at the 7th meeting as a "Constitutional commitment for the Central Government to provide hundred per cent compensation"; the member from Jammu and Kashmir as "an insurance at 14 per cent... even if a State suffered from a calamity".
whatHappened: The Council's own 54th-meeting ledger records ₹6,64,203 crore of compensation paid against ₹7,74,441 crore of cess collected to August 2024. The 14 per cent rate was deliberately set above any defensible projection of nominal growth and was held uniform: the Council refused Meghalaya's request for 18 per cent for the North-East at its 8th meeting precisely to hold that line. The same 8th meeting decided that any shortfall in the Fund would be met by "borrowing from the market which could be repaid by collection of cess in the sixth year or further subsequent year" — a decision the Council's own Secretary assured members need not be legislated, and which was accordingly omitted from the Act. In 2020 the Union relied on its absence from the Act.
assessmentNote: Contested because the evidence supports more than one defensible reading of whether the guarantee was honoured, and the record does not choose. The Union's ledger shows the money paid; the states' record shows a substantial part of it arriving as debt raised in their own name after the Union declined to fund the Fund, under an arrangement the Council never recommended. Both accounts rest on documents that say what each side says they say.
caseFor: A single national rate, uniform across states, is administrable and resists rent-seeking, and the Council held the line against a regional exception in its eighth meeting. The 14 per cent was set generously on purpose, to make an irreversible constitutional reform politically possible; the Chairperson said openly that it exceeded growth plus inflation. Payment was bi-monthly and formulaic, not discretionary. And the promise was kept in cash: ₹6.64 lakh crore was paid, in a period containing the deepest output contraction in India's recorded history, and the states received it while the Union's own revenue fell further than theirs.
caseAgainst: A guaranteed 14 per cent nominal growth locked in the FY2015-16 revenue ranking of states for five years regardless of subsequent performance and, because it was set above any plausible growth path, guaranteed that the cess would be structurally inadequate in any year short of a boom. That inadequacy was foreseen inside the Council and provided for at the 8th meeting by a decision to borrow against future cess; the Council's own officer advised that the decision need not be legislated; and the Union then relied on its absence from the legislation when the shortfall arrived. That is not an inference — it is Punjab's argument, minuted at the 41st meeting with the minute and page cited. The states surrendered the bulk of their independent indirect-tax power permanently in exchange for a five-year insurance whose economic content was left entirely below the constitutional level, with no starting date, no rate and no base year in the Amendment Act, and which expired without any body having to decide that it should.
differentFactsNote: The two sides count different instruments, not one instrument differently. The Union's case rests on the text of the GST (Compensation to States) Act 2017, which contains a five-year transition period and no borrowing obligation. The states' case rests on the minutes of the 8th and 10th Council meetings, which record a decision that shortfall would be met by borrowing repaid from an extended cess, and an assurance that it need not be legislated. Both documents exist, both say what each side says they say, and granting either side's strongest fact in full leaves the other's intact. No common measure could place a statutory text and a minuted decision on one ledger: which instrument governs is a legal question, and it has never been adjudicated because the Article 279A(11) mechanism was never established.

title: The 2020 rupture: the Attorney-General's opinion, the two-bucket split, and an arrangement the GST Council never recommended
summary: At the 41st GST Council meeting on 27 August 2020, convened solely on compensation, the Union tabled the Attorney-General's opinion that "there is no express provision in the Compensation Act which puts a mandate on the Government of India to raise resources or to arrange resources for payment of compensation", while conceding that the states' entitlement was "very hard coded in the Act". The Union proposed splitting the FY2020-21 shortfall of about ₹3,00,000 crore into about ₹1,65,000 crore attributable to GST implementation and about ₹1,35,000 crore attributable to COVID, and offered two borrowing options, in both of which the borrowing was to be in the states' name.
whatHappened: By 12 October 2020 twenty-three states and Union Territories had opted for Option 1, none for Option 2, and eight states plus the National Capital Territory of Delhi had refused both: Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Kerala, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, West Bengal and Delhi. Four states demanded a division at the 42nd meeting; none was held; agenda item 9A closed with no decision recorded. The Union subsequently borrowed itself and on-lent ₹1.1 lakh crore in FY2020-21 and ₹1.59 lakh crore in FY2021-22, at an average execution cost of 4.85 per cent, with a 0.5 per cent borrowing-limit relaxation and an agreement that the debt would not count against the states for Finance Commission norms. Tamil Nadu's own accounts record the treatment: ₹6,241 crore and ₹8,095.25 crore booked under Major Head 6004 Public Debt and excluded from every debt indicator by a Department of Expenditure decision.
assessmentNote: Contested on the record's own terms. One of the three factual disputes is resolvable and resolves against the Union — the 42nd minutes contain a decision on agenda item 9 and none on 9A, so the arrangement was implemented without a Council recommendation. The other two are legal questions about what the Compensation Act contains and whether a Council decision survives its omission from a statute, and no instrument in the corpus answers either, because the Article 279A(11) adjudication mechanism does not exist.
caseFor: The Compensation Act compensates loss "arising on account of implementation of" GST, and a once-in-a-century pandemic is not implementation. The Union's own revenue fell further than the states' — the Finance Secretary made the point at the 41st meeting and Delhi conceded it. The statute creates a Fund, not a Union liability, and the Attorney-General so advised. The Union nonetheless found the money: it extended the cess, arranged a special Reserve Bank window executed at 4.85 per cent, far below any state's own market cost, relaxed borrowing limits, agreed the debt would be invisible to Finance Commission norms, and — having first insisted the states borrow — borrowed itself and on-lent the whole amount. Twenty-three of thirty-one members accepted, including every North-Eastern state, and Andhra Pradesh's minuted objection to the mechanism ends with it opting in.
caseAgainst: The Act's operative machinery contains no causal test — compensation is protected revenue minus actual revenue — and the Attorney-General said so in the first limb of the very opinion the Union relied on. Splitting the shortfall into causal buckets inserts a condition the statute does not contain, and Kerala said exactly that on the record: "the Constitution does not make such distinction... there is no distinction made in legal terms". The 8th meeting had already decided the shortfall would be met by borrowing repaid from an extended cess, and the Union's own officer had assured the Council it need not be legislated. The options were then communicated to states directly by the Department of Expenditure, bypassing the Council; Punjab's objection that the "Council otherwise doesn't have the power to alter the compensation mechanism suo motto" was never answered. And four states' demand for the one constitutional remedy available to them, a division, was simply not put.
differentFactsNote: The two sides rely on different instruments and neither contradicts the other's factual claim. The Union's case is grounded in the Act's text and a law officer's opinion on it; the states' is grounded in Council minutes recording a decision that was deliberately not legislated. Both documents exist and neither is disputed. Which instrument governs is a legal question that no ledger of rupees can bridge. The one sub-question that IS resolvable from the record — whether the Council recommended the borrowing arrangement — is resolved here and against the Union, and it does not dispose of the other two.

title: The compensation cess outlives the compensation: an open-ended Council recommendation implemented as a fixed date by notification
summary: At its 42nd meeting on 12 October 2020 the GST Council "approved to extend the levy of Compensation Cess beyond June 2022 till the entire shortfall is covered" — an open-ended recommendation carried by consensus, with Kerala, West Bengal, Punjab, Karnataka, Puducherry, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Goa and Odisha each minuted in support. The terminal date of 31 March 2026 was then fixed by executive notification, not by the Council. The Chairperson said so at the 54th meeting: "the period for levy was extended to March, 2026 by way of notification based on an opinion taken from the Attorney General of India."
whatHappened: The cess became a separate instrument from the guarantee it was created to fund. The guarantee ended on 30 June 2022; the cess continued, to service about ₹2.69 lakh crore of principal and about ₹51,561 crore of interest on the back-to-back loans. The 45th meeting's own arithmetic shows the date is an amortisation calculation rather than a policy horizon. Because Option 1 clause XI made interest the first charge and principal the second, the states' compensation arrears ranked behind debt service on a borrowing the Council never approved.
assessmentNote: Contested because both readings of the same documents are defensible: section 8(1) of the Compensation Act does contemplate extension "for such period as may be prescribed on the recommendations of the Council", and what the Council recommended was open-ended while what was notified was a date. Neither reading misstates the record.
caseFor: Section 8(1) provides for the cess for five years "or for such period as may be prescribed on the recommendations of the Council" — extension by notification on a Council recommendation is exactly the mechanism the statute contemplates. The Council recommended it unanimously, and without it the arrears could not have been paid at all. Fixing a terminal date by delegated legislation is the ordinary route; an open-ended levy with no end date would have been worse for taxpayers and would have left the states with no visibility of when their own consumers stop paying.
caseAgainst: The Council recommended an extension tied to a condition — "till the entire shortfall is covered" — and what was notified was a date tied to a debt-amortisation schedule. Those are different objects, and the second was fixed by the Union alone on its own law officer's advice. Punjab had asked at the 42nd meeting that "the end date should not be defined and the levy should be extended till full compensation is settled"; the notification did the opposite. And clause XI's priority order means a levy the states supported in order to recover their arrears was applied first to servicing the substitute for those arrears — so the states funded, out of a cess on their own consumers, the interest on a loan raised because the Union declined to fund the Fund.
differentFactsNote: Both sides accept the Council's decision text, the notification, the law officer's advice and clause XI's priority order. The disagreement is whether fixing a terminal date by notification is faithful implementation of an open-ended recommendation, which is a weighting of one agreed record.

title: Sixteen members asked the GST Council to extend compensation and the minutes record no answer
summary: At the 47th GST Council meeting on 28-29 June 2022, two days before the compensation guarantee expired, agenda item 22 was listed as a "General Discussion on Compensation". Sixteen states and Union Territories asked on the record for the guarantee to be extended, across every party grouping and including six states governed by the Union's own party. The minutes record no Chairperson's response on extension, no decision, no deferral, no reference to a Group of Ministers and no refusal. The item is followed immediately by the vote of thanks. The guarantee lapsed the next day by effluxion of time.
assessmentNote: The agenda item carried no proposal — it was listed as a discussion, which is why no decision was capable of being taken on it — so no objective was stated at announcement against which anything could be scored. What the record finds is the absence of a recorded disposal, and that is firmly established from the minute book itself.
caseFor: The five-year term is fixed by section 18 of the 101st Amendment and by the Act's own definition of the transition period; extending it would require Parliament to legislate afresh, which is not within the Council's gift, so there was no recommendation the Council was competent to make and nothing to put. The money question was already answered on the record: the Secretary told the 45th meeting that cess collections to March 2026 were fully committed to servicing about ₹2.69 lakh crore of principal, about ₹51,561 crore of interest and the outstanding arrears, so there was no resource to extend with. The states had received the benefit of a 14 per cent guarantee through a pandemic and the Union's ledger shows ₹6.64 lakh crore paid.
caseAgainst: A request made by sixteen of thirty-one members, in a constitutional body whose decisions are taken by weighted vote, was disposed of by not being put. Had it been put and lost, the record would show which members opposed it and at what weight; had it been put and won, it would have been a recommendation the Union would have had to answer. Listing the item as a "General Discussion" removed the possibility of either. The demand was cross-party — Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh all asked — so the absence of a recorded disposal cannot be explained as the Council declining a partisan demand. And Tamil Nadu's version was not a demand for the same money at all: it asked to continue the scheme with the 14 per cent baseline reset downwards, which meets the affordability objection head-on and is addressed nowhere in the minutes.
differentFactsNote: Both sides accept the agenda listing, the sixteen requests and the absence of any recorded response. The disagreement is whether a body that cannot grant a request owes it a recorded refusal, which is a weighting of an agreed record.

title: The GST Council's constitutional dispute-adjudication mechanism has never been established
summary: Article 279A(11) provides that the GST Council "shall establish a mechanism to adjudicate any dispute" between the Union and one or more states, or between states, arising out of the Council's recommendations or their implementation. Ten years after the Council was constituted, no such mechanism exists. Activation has been formally demanded in Council at least four times by named members on named dates, and the Council's own committees index lists no adjudicating body.
claimAtLaunch: The constitutional text itself: to adjudicate disputes arising out of the Council's recommendations or their implementation.
whatHappened: Punjab raised it at the 37th meeting on 20 September 2019, as recalled in the 39th minutes; a member raised "activating the dispute resolution mechanism" at the 38th meeting on 18 December 2019; Punjab at the 39th meeting on 14 March 2020 said "the time has become ripe to activate the dispute resolution mechanism envisaged in the Constitution under Article 279A and requested that this Agenda may be brought in the next meeting of the Council"; and Punjab at the 42nd meeting on 12 October 2020 "requested that in a time bound manner, the dispute resolution mechanism may be set up in 7 days... Alternatively, he suggested that the possibility of formation of GoM on the issue may also be explored." The Council's committees index lists the Fitment Committee, the Law Committee, two Groups of Officers, the GST Implementation Committee, a Grievances Redressal Committee, a State Coordination Committee, an All India Coordination Committee and an IT Grievance Redressal Committee. None adjudicates a Centre-state dispute: the Grievances Redressal Committee is a taxpayer body and the GST Appellate Tribunal hears taxpayer appeals under Chapter XVIII of the CGST Act.
assessmentNote: Failed against the objective stated in the constitutional text that created the duty. The mechanism is non-establishment over ten years despite four recorded demands — not a court striking anything down, and not a withdrawal by the enacting authority. The word "shall" in Article 279A(11) is the objective; the empty committees index is the outcome.
caseFor: Article 279A(11) says the Council shall establish a mechanism and leaves the form, timing and trigger entirely to the Council, a body of thirty-one governments deciding by three-quarters weighted majority — so a mechanism can exist only if the states themselves, who hold two-thirds of the weight, carry it, and they have never put it to a vote. In practice the Council has divided once in nine years and worked by consensus in fifty-four other meetings, which is what a dispute mechanism would have been for. Disputes that could not be settled in Council have gone to the Supreme Court under Articles 131 and 32 and been heard there, so no state has been left without a forum. And building an adjudicating body inside a body whose Chairperson is a party would have raised its own objection.
caseAgainst: The Constitution uses the mandatory "shall", and the duty sits on a Council the Union chairs and whose agenda the Union controls; four recorded demands by a named member across three years produced no agenda item. The consequence is precise and visible in the other records of this phase: when the compensation dispute of 2020 turned on whether the Compensation Act contains a causal test and whether an unlegislated Council decision survives, there was no forum inside the design to answer it, and there still is none. A body in which the Centre alone holds a blocking third, in which no group of states can reach the 75 per cent threshold over the Chairperson's objection, and in which the only counterweight the Constitution provides has not been built, is not a shared sovereignty in the respect that matters most — what happens when the sharing fails.
differentFactsNote: Both sides accept the text of Article 279A(11), the four demands, their dates and the contents of the committees index. The disagreement is about whether a duty on a collective body can be breached by the party that chairs it, which is an argument about responsibility for an agreed fact.

title: Ten Tamil Nadu bills deemed assented by the Supreme Court, and the doctrine that assented them withdrawn seven months later
summary: Twelve bills passed by the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly between 13 January 2020 and 28 April 2023 sat with the Governor for between 199 and 1,400 days. He acted on all twelve on 13 November 2023, three days after the Supreme Court issued notice on the State's writ petition, withholding assent to ten without any message for reconsideration and reserving two for the President. The Assembly repassed the ten in a special session on 18 November 2023; the Governor reserved them for the President ten days later. On 8 April 2025 the Supreme Court held the second-round reservation illegal, set aside the President's consequent actions and, under Article 142, declared the ten bills deemed assented as of 18 November 2023 — the only instance in Indian constitutional history in which assent has been deemed. On 13 May 2025 the President referred fourteen questions under Article 143. On 20 November 2025 a Constitution Bench held that the Governor is not bound by ministerial advice under Article 200, that the function is not justiciable on its merits, that courts may not prescribe timelines, and that the Constitution, "Article 142 even, does not allow for the concept of 'deemed assent' of Bills" — while expressly declining to disturb the relief already granted to Tamil Nadu.
whatHappened: The ten Acts stand. The doctrine that produced them does not, and no state can use it again. What survives on the states' side is a limited mandamus where inaction is "prolonged, unexplained, and indefinite" — a standard the Court did not define — and the holding that Article 361 immunises the person of the Governor but not the office.
assessmentNote: Contested because the two sides do not disagree about a single fact. Every date is admitted, and most of them were supplied by the Governor. The dispute is entirely about what Article 200 permits, and the Supreme Court gave two answers to that in seven months. Not awaiting-adjudication: the adjudication has happened, twice, and the record carries both.
caseFor: Article 200 confers a constitutional function on the Governor with no time limit written into it, and a Constitution Bench has now held the absence deliberate: the framers wrote deeming clauses into Articles 107, 108, 109(4), 109(5), 196, 197, 198(4), 198(5), 213 and 239B and wrote none into 200 or 201. "In the absence of constitutionally prescribed time limits, and the manner of exercise of power by the Governor, it would not be appropriate for this Court to judicially prescribe timelines." A two-judge Bench had read into Article 200 a timetable the Constitution does not contain and then enforced it with a remedy — deemed assent — that the larger Bench characterised as "virtually a takeover, and substitution, of the executive functions by the Judiciary". The bills at issue transferred the appointment of Vice-Chancellors from the Governor as Chancellor to the State Government, a subject on which Entry 66 of List I gives the Union a genuine interest, and reserving such bills for the President is the constitutional route for resolving exactly that question. The five-judge opinion also left Tamil Nadu's relief intact, which is the opposite of vindictiveness.
caseAgainst: The measured facts are not in dispute and were supplied by the Governor himself: 199 to 1,400 days of silence, ended three days after the Supreme Court issued notice, and a second-round reservation completed in ten days. Whatever Article 200 permits, a function performed in ten days when a court is watching and not at all for nearly four years when it is not is not a considered exercise of discretion. The bills were passed by an elected legislature, repassed without material change after the first refusal, and every one of them concerns universities the State funds. After 20 November 2025 the position is that this can recur with no timeline, no merits review, no duty to give reasons, no duty even to announce the decision, and no remedy beyond an undefined mandamus. Tamil Nadu's Acts survive; the mechanism that produced them does not.
differentFactsNote: The clearest weighting case in the phase and the one most likely to be misread as a different-facts case. Nobody disputes that Article 200 has no time limit; nobody disputes that ten bills sat for over a year; nobody disputes the dates of the second-round reservation. The two sides differ on the weight to give the framers' silence, not on what the framers wrote or on what the Governor did.

title: The Constitution sets a deadline for the elected legislature and none for the Union's appointee, and both sides argue from the same silence
summary: Article 200 gives the Governor three options on a bill presented to him — assent, withhold assent, or reserve it for the President — and attaches the words "as soon as possible" only to returning a bill for reconsideration. Article 201 gives the President two options and no period at all. The single fixed period in the whole scheme is six months, and it binds the State legislature to reconsider a returned bill. There is no deeming provision, no lapse and no default anywhere in the scheme. After 20 November 2025 there is also no judicially enforceable clock, no merits review, no duty to give reasons and no duty to announce the decision.
whatHappened: The Punjab judgment records at paragraph 8 that "the Governor did not 'declare' in any public notification that he is withholding his assent to the Bills" — so the deciding officer need not announce the decision, and no register follows from the Constitution. The measurable consequence is that no national count of bills pending with Governors exists: neither the April 2025 judgment nor the November 2025 Constitution Bench opinion cites any aggregate figure, and a Constitution Bench decided the legal effect of a quantity without either party placing a national figure for it before the Court. What exists instead is bill-by-bill, state-by-state, only for litigated states, and only at the moment of litigation: twelve rows for Tamil Nadu, eight named bills for Kerala with a pendency range of seven to twenty-three months, four bills plus three Money Bills for Punjab.
assessmentNote: No objective was stated at announcement because the subject is a constitutional design, not a measure. The record finds something real and firmly established — an asymmetry in the text, and the absence of any register following from it — and there is no claim to score. The value asserts nothing about the finding's quality.
caseFor: The framers wrote deeming clauses into ten other Articles and none into 200 or 201, and a five-judge Bench found that decisive. The office is a constitutional check, not a postbox: the second proviso to Article 200 makes reservation mandatory in a defined case, which shows the framers contemplated the Governor stopping a bill. The elasticity is deliberate — "The text of Articles 200 and 201, has been framed in such a manner, so as to provide a sense of elasticity" — and the considerations the function serves are, in the Union's own words in the Presidential Reference, "polycentric considerations, inter alia being federalism, uniformity of laws, integrity and security of the nation, doctrine of separation of powers". A deadline on a discretion is a different constitution from the one that was written, and amending it is Parliament's work, not a court's.
caseAgainst: "Shall declare" admits of no inaction, and a power with no stated period must be exercised in reasonable time. The concrete consequence of the contrary reading was stated by the Court itself in 2023: an unelected appointee "would be in a position to virtually veto the functioning of the legislative domain by a duly elected legislature by simply declaring that assent is withheld without any further recourse". The measured facts support the concern — 1,400 days in Tamil Nadu, seven to twenty-three months in Kerala — and the six-month clock the Constitution does contain runs against the elected House, not against the appointee. Three official commissions have recommended fixing the gap and none has been implemented.
differentFactsNote: Every fact in both cases is agreed: the text, the absence of deeming clauses, the dates in each litigated state, and the holdings of both 2025 benches. The two sides differ on the weight to give the framers' silence. This is the structural statement that distinguishes the assent dispute from the fiscal disputes in this phase, where the parties genuinely disagree about a subtraction.

title: Delhi: a Constitution Bench holding reversed by statute in eight days, under an express constitutional licence to do so
summary: On 11 May 2023 a Constitution Bench held that the Government of the National Capital Territory of Delhi has legislative and executive power over Services and that the Lieutenant Governor is bound by the Council of Ministers on them. On 19 May 2023 — eight days later — Part IV-A of the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act took effect, creating a National Capital Civil Service Authority, making its subject matter one on which the Lieutenant Governor acts "in his sole discretion", and providing that on a difference of opinion "the decision of the Lieutenant Governor shall be final". It was carried into permanent law by Act 19 of 2023.
claimAtLaunch: The Part's own heading is the only objective statement retrieved: "PROVISIONS RELATING TO THE MAINTENANCE OF THE DEMOCRATIC AND ADMINISTRATIVE BALANCE IN THE GOVERNANCE OF NATIONAL CAPITAL TERRITORY OF DELHI".
assessmentNote: Contested because both readings rest on the same admitted text and the same dates. The measure was not struck down and was not withdrawn, so neither failed nor reversed applies; and the constitutional question it raises has been answered — Article 239AA(7)(b) authorises it — so nothing is awaiting adjudication.
caseFor: Article 239AA(7)(b) expressly authorises exactly this: a law made under 239AA(7)(a) "shall not be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368 notwithstanding that it contains any provision which amends or has the effect of amending, this Constitution." The framers of that clause contemplated Parliament legislating around the constitutional arrangement for Delhi, and Delhi is the national capital: the Union's stake in the administration of the seat of government is not a pretext. The 2023 Bench itself described Delhi as sui generis — a category Parliament may legislate for — and the Authority is chaired by the Chief Minister, not by the Lieutenant Governor.
caseAgainst: The 2023 Bench held the executive power of the National Capital Territory "co-extensive with its legislative power", and the statute that followed eight days later made the very subject of that holding one on which the Lieutenant Governor acts in his sole discretion. A three-member Authority chaired by the Chief Minister but including a Chief Secretary appointed by the Central Government, deciding by majority, can outvote the elected head two to one on his own officers — and even its recommendation is subject to the Lieutenant Governor's final say. An express licence to legislate around a judgment is not an argument for using it the week after one. And Delhi votes as a State in the GST Council, so the Union treats the same government as a state for fiscal purposes and as a subordinate administration for its own civil service.
differentFactsNote: Unusually clean as a weighting case: both sides accept the text of Article 239AA(7)(b), the dates, the composition of the Authority and the terms of the 2023 holding. The disagreement is entirely about whether an express constitutional licence should be used eight days after a judgment.

title: Article 356 since 2014: four proclamations outside Jammu and Kashmir, and no official list of any of them
summary: Excluding Jammu and Kashmir, which the phase-12 records own, Article 356 has been invoked four times since May 2014: Arunachal Pradesh from 26 January 2016 for about twenty-four days, Uttarakhand from 27 March 2016 for about forty-five days, Maharashtra from 12 November 2019 for about eleven days, and Manipur from 13 February 2025 to 4 February 2026 — about 357 days. Puducherry in 2021 is not in this list: it was section 51 of the Government of Union Territories Act 1963, a different statute. The Ministry of Home Affairs, whose own Annual Report describes "imposition of President's Rule" as part of its Centre-State Division's mandate, has never published a list of Article 356 proclamations in any Annual Report checked, and its Centre-State Division page carries none.
whatHappened: For Uttarakhand and Maharashtra the instrument is the Rajya Sabha laying record under Article 356(3), which names the Proclamation's G.S.R. number, the accompanying Order, and separately lays "the Report of the Governor... recommending the issue of the Proclamation". That laying record is a genuine one-ledger instrument: the Union's proclamation and the Governor's report go before the House together. For Arunachal Pradesh 2016 and Manipur 2025 no such record was obtained, and no Gazette notification was read for any of the four. The last official cumulative figure of any kind is the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution's count of 111 invocations as at 2002 — which expressly bundles thirteen applications of section 51 of the Government of Union Territories Act with Article 356 proper, and subtracts ten applied "technically due to the mechanics of the Constitution", leaving 54 with "apparent circumstances to warrant invocation", 13 of "possible misuse" and 18 of "clear misuse".
assessmentNote: No objective was stated at announcement: a proclamation is an exercise of a constitutional power, not a measure with a claimed outcome, and no Union document states what any of the four was to achieve. The record's finding is the absence of an official register, which is firmly established by a sweep of the nodal ministry's own Annual Reports and division page.
caseFor: Every proclamation is laid before both Houses within two months under Article 356(3) and must be approved by resolution of Parliament, so Parliament is the register and a ministry list would be duplicative. Four invocations in twelve years, three of them lasting between eleven and forty-five days, is a marked restraint against the historical record the NCRWC counted; on that count the power was used 111 times in the first fifty-two years. The one long proclamation, Manipur, followed sustained civil conflict, which is the circumstance Article 356 was written for.
caseAgainst: A laying record is a scatter of individual entries across decades of debates, findable only if you already know the date — which is exactly what a series is for and exactly what is missing. The nodal ministry names the subject in its own mandate and publishes no list, so the count in this record had to be assembled from two Rajya Sabha debate volumes and two rows that have no T1 instrument at all. The only cumulative figure that exists is twenty-four years old and mixes two statutes, so no published number separates Article 356 from section 51 of the Government of Union Territories Act, and any modern count that adds Puducherry 2021 to Uttarakhand 2016 is doing the same bundling without saying so.
differentFactsNote: Both sides accept the four instances, the laying requirement and the absence of a ministry list. The disagreement is whether parliamentary laying discharges the duty of record, which is a weighting of an agreed record.
