title: Three commissions recommended consulting the Chief Minister on the appointment of Governors; the Inter-State Council has met eleven times in thirty-six years and not once in the last ten
summary: The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution recommended in 2002 that a Governor be appointed "after consultation with the Chief Minister of that State", that removal or transfer follow a similar procedure, that the Sarkaria criteria be applied, and that assent be subject to time limits. Sarkaria (1988) had held that the Governor "must abide by the advice of his Council of Ministers" under Article 200 save in rare and exceptional cases of patent unconstitutionality. Punchhi (2010) held that "concrete timelines are sine qua non". None has been implemented. Punchhi's 273 recommendations went to the eleventh meeting of the Inter-State Council on 16 July 2016, which referred them to its Standing Committee; the Standing Committee met on 9 April 2017, 25 November 2017 and 25 May 2018. The Ministry of Home Affairs Annual Report 2024-25 then states: "It has been decided to obtain updated comments of the State Governments/UT Administrations on the recommendations of the Standing Committee. In view of this, a meeting of the ISC to discuss the Punchhi Commission recommendations could not be held."
assessmentNote: No objective was stated at announcement. The Annual Report states a status, not an objective, and no Union document has ever claimed that the commissions' recommendations would be implemented by a date or at all. The finding — a constitutional consultative forum that has met eleven times in thirty-six years and not once in the last ten — is firmly established from the ministry's own report.
caseFor: Article 155 confers the appointment power on the President without qualification, and adding a consultation requirement is a constitutional amendment, not an administrative decision — Punchhi itself advocated implementation "by way of a Constitutional Amendment". The Inter-State Council is a consultative body of the States themselves, and it was the Chief Ministers who asked in 2016 that the Standing Committee examine the recommendations first, so the delay is, on the Union's own record, a delay the States asked for. The recommendations are also not costless: consultation on the appointment of a constitutional functionary whose function includes reserving a State's bills for the President would give the government whose bills are at stake a say in choosing the officer who decides.
caseAgainst: The forum has met eleven times in thirty-six years and not once in the last ten. A body that does not meet cannot decide, and a recommendation referred to a committee of a body that does not meet is not under consideration in any meaningful sense. The stated reason for the latest non-meeting is that updated comments are being obtained — a process that has run for eight years since the Standing Committee last met. And the two documents most cited in every Governor debate in India, the Sarkaria and Punchhi reports, could not be read at all in this run: interstatecouncil.gov.in resolves but its port 443 is closed and no Wayback capture of any chapter returns 200, so both are known here only through what the NCRWC report and the Supreme Court quote of them.
differentFactsNote: Both sides would accept every date, every recommendation and the ministry's own account of why the Council has not met. The disagreement is about whether an unfinished process that has been unfinished for eight years is consideration or its absence.

title: West Bengal's MGNREGA money stopped under section 27 on 9 March 2022, and restored by a court rather than by the Ministry
summary: Section 27 of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 allowed the Central Government, on a complaint about the issue or improper utilisation of funds and if "prima facie satisfied that there is a case", to "order stoppage of release of funds to the Scheme". Central release to West Bengal stopped on 9 March 2022 and did not resume for more than four years. The Union's own by-state table shows releases of ₹11,454.05 crore in FY2020-21, ₹7,507.80 crore in FY2021-22 and ₹0.00 in FY2022-23. Restoration came from the Calcutta High Court, not from the Ministry: an order of 18 June 2025, departmental orders of 6 December 2025, and resumption with effect from 1 June 2026.
whatHappened: The Union's stated ground is inspection findings of financial misappropriation, execution of non-permissible activities, splitting of works and lack of transparency, and non-compliance with Central Government directives. The antecedent step was an unapproved upward revision of the State's labour budget for FY2021-22. New job cards issued in West Bengal fell from 16.82 lakh in FY2020-21 to 8.25 lakh and then 2.15 lakh — but Bihar, against which no stoppage was ordered, fell from 26.68 lakh to 11.37 lakh over the same two years, so the series cannot separate the stoppage from whatever else was moving. The power has been used once, against one state, and the Union has told the Lok Sabha in terms that no direction under section 27 was issued to Tamil Nadu.
assessmentNote: Contested rather than failed: the two sides weight the same facts differently and no instrument in the record adjudicates between a proportionate enforcement action and a disproportionate one. The section 27 order itself has never been published, so the reasons that would settle it are not on any record.
caseFor: Section 27 is a statute passed by Parliament, and Parliament wrote the power into a scheme that spends Union money in a state the Union does not administer. The threshold is a complaint plus prima facie satisfaction, and the Union has stated the ground on the record and repeatedly: central team inspections in nineteen districts finding financial misappropriation, non-permissible works and splitting of works. The power has been used once in twenty years, which is not a pattern. The stoppage runs to the Scheme, not to the State, and every other central scheme continued; the Union's own account is that more than ₹1.10 lakh crore has gone to West Bengal for rural development since FY2014-15. And the State's own conduct is in the record too: the Union complains that a centrally funded housing scheme was renamed, and an unapproved labour-budget revision preceded the stoppage.
caseAgainst: The power runs, on its own words, to "the Scheme", and there is no notice, no hearing, no time limit, no ceiling and no appeal in the section — "prima facie satisfied" is the entire threshold. It was used for fifty-one months against one state, and released only when a High Court ordered it. A statutory entitlement to a hundred days' work was suspended for the population of a state on the strength of findings in nineteen districts, and no instrument states why the whole state rather than the nineteen districts. Wages are a Union liability under the Act and the pending liability the Union itself acknowledges includes a wage component. And the order itself has never been published: the Union describes it in Parliament and does not produce it, so the reasons cannot be tested by anyone.
differentFactsNote: The dates, the statutory provision, the release figures and the inspection findings are all the Union's own, and the State does not contest the release figures. The disagreement is about proportionality and about who bore the cost — which is a weighting of one agreed record, not two ledgers. The one thing that would settle it, the section 27 order with its reasons, is unpublished, and its absence bears on both sides equally.

title: MGNREGA is repealed: the unskilled wage moves from 100 per cent Central to 60:40 and the fund-stopping power survives near-verbatim
summary: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 stands repealed with effect from 1 July 2026 by the Viksit Bharat — Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act 2025, Act No. 36 of 2025, enacted 20 December 2025 with commencement notified for 11 May 2026. This is a statute passed by Parliament, not an executive act. Under MGNREGA section 22(1)(a) the unskilled wage was 100 per cent Central, unqualified, with no State share at all; under the new Act the unskilled wage appears in both the Central and the State limbs of section 22 and is subsumed into a 60:40 split, 90:10 for the North-Eastern and Himalayan states. The guarantee moves from 100 days to 125, but a statutory sixty-day peak-season blackout means the 125 days must be delivered inside 305. The fund-stopping power carries over as section 29, differing from MGNREGA section 27(2) by two words and a comma.
claimAtLaunch: A raised guarantee of 125 days of work.
assessmentNote: The repeal took effect on 1 July 2026 and the record is dated five weeks later. The obstacle is elapsed time and the evidence time accumulates — whether 125 days are in fact delivered inside 305, and whether states meet a 40 per cent share of the unskilled wage they never previously bore, are questions only outturn answers. Not awaiting-adjudication: nothing is pending before any body outside Parliament.
caseFor: Parliament may repeal and replace its own statute, and it raised the guarantee by a quarter in doing so. Cost-sharing on the unskilled wage brings the largest rural scheme into line with the ordinary centrally sponsored scheme ratio and gives states a financial stake in the quality of the works they choose and supervise — which is the Union's standing answer to every complaint about scheme design, and it is the answer the Fourteenth Finance Commission itself endorsed when it moved money from grants to untied devolution. A peak-season blackout is an agricultural-labour-market measure, not a reduction: it prevents a public works programme from competing with the harvest for the same workers.
caseAgainst: The change moves a statutory liability the Union bore alone onto state budgets, in a scheme whose demand the state cannot control, and it does so in the same instrument that raises the entitlement — so the states carry 40 per cent of a larger number. The demand-driven character goes with it: a capped normative allocation with the overrun on the state is not a guarantee in the sense the old Act used the word. And the one provision that is not reformed at all is the power to stop the money: section 29 reproduces section 27(2) almost word for word, with no notice, no hearing, no time limit, no ceiling and no appeal added, in the same year in which a High Court had to order that power's effects reversed after fifty-one months.
differentFactsNote: Both sides accept the statutory text, the ratios, the day counts and the carry-over of the stoppage power. The disagreement is whether cost-sharing on a demand-driven entitlement is accountability or transfer of risk, which is a weighting of one agreed instrument.

title: ₹30,085 crore a year reaches Tamil Nadu without passing through Tamil Nadu's budget, and its auditor says the State's accounts are untrue to that extent
summary: The Government of India transfers funds directly to State Implementing Agencies in Tamil Nadu — societies, corporations and missions authorised by the State to receive central money — without routing them through the State Budget or the State Treasury. The amount rose monotonically from ₹3,914.73 crore in FY2015-16 to ₹30,085.53 crore in FY2023-24, with MGNREGS at ₹10,254.44 crore the largest single line in the final year. The Comptroller and Auditor General records in each of six consecutive State Finances Audit Reports that the Annual Finance Accounts do not capture this flow, and concludes that the State's receipts, expenditure and every fiscal parameter derived from them "did not present the true and fair picture to that extent".
whatHappened: The CAG also records that a Government of India decision of 8 July 2015 required all centrally sponsored scheme assistance to be released to the State Government and not directly to implementing agencies, and that MGNREGS money has nonetheless been released directly to agencies in Tamil Nadu since FY2015-16. The quantum comes from the Union's own Public Financial Management System, operated by the Controller General of Accounts, and is set by the auditor against the State's Finance Accounts.
assessmentNote: Contested, with the quantum not in dispute at all: it is the Union's own PFMS figure reproduced by the auditor. The dispute is about whether bypassing a State legislature's appropriation is a defect. This is the cleanest instance in the phase of an agreed number with a disputed meaning.
caseFor: Direct transfer to an implementing agency is faster, is tracked end to end in the Union's own payment system, reduces float in State treasuries, and is disclosed: the CAG's own figures come from the Union's system and the scheme-level detail is published in the State Finance Accounts every year. Nothing is concealed, and the money is spent in the State on schemes the State administers. The 2015 decision is an administrative preference about routing, not a statutory entitlement of the State treasury, and what a State's Finance Accounts capture is determined by the State's own accounting choices.
caseAgainst: A legislature appropriates what passes through its Consolidated Fund. ₹30,085 crore that never enters the State Budget is ₹30,085 crore the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly neither votes nor scrutinises, spent by bodies it does not appropriate to. The consequence is not rhetorical: the auditor states in terms that the State's published fiscal aggregates are not true and fair to that extent, which means every debt, deficit and transfer ratio computed for Tamil Nadu — including the ones the Union cites — rests on an incomplete base. And the Union has departed from its own written decision of 8 July 2015 for nine consecutive years on the largest scheme, without recording a reason anywhere the auditor could find.
differentFactsNote: One number, two meanings. The quantum originates with the Union, is reported by a third institution and is not contested by anyone; what is contested is whether money that reaches its purpose without reaching the legislature is properly spent. No second ledger exists because none is needed.

unmeasured.why: The Union unquestionably holds the number by State and by scheme — the auditor obtains it from the Union's own payment system — but no routine Union publication of it by State was found. The Union Budget's transfers statement carries no by-state breakdown at all, and the one state-by-scheme-by-year disclosure retrievable in this run was a parliamentary answer: disclosure is on demand, not by publication. This drop did not sweep the Union side exhaustively and must not be read as having closed the question.

title: Tamil Nadu received ₹50,700.69 crore of GST compensation and never passed ₹5,070.06 crore of it to its own local bodies
summary: Between FY2018-19 and FY2023-24 the Government of India released ₹50,700.69 crore of GST compensation to Tamil Nadu. Tamil Nadu's own Fifth State Finance Commission recommended, and the State Government accepted, that ten per cent of it — ₹5,070.06 crore — be transferred to local bodies. It was never transferred, and the Department admitted so at the audit exit conference. The same state's auditor separately recomputed the protected revenue Tamil Nadu was owed from the statutory base year and found the compensation received fell short of the guarantee: shortfalls of ₹455.16 crore for July 2017 to March 2018, ₹2,445.71 crore for FY2018-19 and ₹3,009.76 crore for FY2019-20.
whatHappened: The CAG built the shortfall from the statute: the FY2015-16 subsumed-tax base of ₹29,786.36 crore compounded at 14 per cent gives a protected FY2018-19 revenue of ₹44,129.80 crore against ₹41,684.09 crore actually collected including compensation, an outturn growth of 7.68 per cent against the protected 14. Part of what Tamil Nadu received was not compensation at all but debt: ₹6,241 crore in FY2020-21 and ₹8,095.25 crore in FY2021-22 were booked as back-to-back loans under Major Head 6004 Public Debt, and the Department of Expenditure decided the amounts "would not be treated as debt of the State for any norms which may be prescribed by the Finance Commission". Tamil Nadu's grants-in-aid from the Union then fell 32.84 per cent in FY2023-24, which the CAG attributes mainly to the cessation of GST compensation from July 2023 and to non-receipt of the Central share of ₹225 crore for the State Disaster Mitigation Fund.
assessmentNote: Contested and authored as ONE record. The receipt and the non-transfer are two halves of a single finding about how money moves down a three-tier federation, and splitting them would let either half be quoted alone — which is the failure this instrument exists to prevent. Both caseFor and caseAgainst carry a State limb and a Union limb; a version of this record with only one of each would be dishonest.
caseFor: On the Union's side: the compensation was paid, in full and on a formula, through a pandemic — ₹50,700.69 crore to one state over six years — and where the Fund could not meet it the Union borrowed at 4.85 per cent and on-lent, then agreed the borrowing would be invisible to Finance Commission debt norms, which is a concession of real value to the State. The guarantee had a statutory end and Tamil Nadu knew the date from 2017. On the State's side: the ten per cent to local bodies was a State Finance Commission recommendation about a receipt whose own continuation the State could not rely on, and a State facing the cessation of the compensation itself has an argument for holding the money at the level that must absorb the shock.
caseAgainst: On the State's side: the auditor's own recomputation from the statutory base shows the compensation received did not restore the protected revenue in any of the three years it could test, so the guarantee under-delivered on its own arithmetic before it expired; and a third of what arrived in two of those years was debt, recorded as public debt in the State's own books. On the Union's side, turned against the State: Tamil Nadu complains that money owed to it was withheld while itself withholding ₹5,070.06 crore owed to its own local bodies under a recommendation its own government accepted, and admitting it only when the auditor asked. A state that argues the Union must honour a fiscal commitment to it cannot decline to honour the identical commitment to the tier below without answering the same argument.
differentFactsNote: Every figure here comes from one institution, the state's own auditor, reading both governments' accounts; nobody disputes any of them. The two cases weight the same ledger. The mirror image is the point: the same conduct is complained of and practised by the same government at two levels of the same federation.

That argument must not be put in Tamil Nadu's mouth.

title: The Union withheld GST transaction data from its own constitutional auditor, which certified a state's accounts on a test basis as a one-time exception
summary: In certifying the Government of Tamil Nadu's accounts for FY2018-19 the Comptroller and Auditor General recorded, in the certificate itself: "The required access to data is yet to be provided. Not having access to the data pertaining to all GST transactions has come in the way of comprehensively auditing the GST Receipts. The accounts for the year 2018-19 are, therefore, certified on the basis of test audit... as a one-time exception." The subject is the GST instrument rather than Tamil Nadu; Tamil Nadu is where the consequence surfaced.
assessmentNote: No objective was stated at announcement: nobody claimed the auditor would or would not be given access, and there is no measure here whose stated purpose could be scored. The record finds something real — a constitutional auditor recording in a certificate that it was not given the data it asked for — and the value asserts nothing about the finding's quality.
caseFor: The GST Network holds taxpayer-level transaction data for the whole country, and access to it is governed by confidentiality obligations that run to taxpayers, not to either government. A state auditor asking for all GST transactions is asking for a national dataset in order to audit one state's receipts, and calibrating that access takes time and rules. The auditor certified the accounts, said what it had done, and did so as a one-time exception — which is the system working: the qualification is on the face of the certificate for anyone to read.
caseAgainst: The Comptroller and Auditor General is a constitutional office under Articles 148 to 151 whose certificate is what makes a state's accounts an account. It asked for the data that would let it audit a receipt head, did not get it, and had to certify a state's accounts on a test basis. Positive control: the same report series certifies every other year without such a caveat, so this is an event and not boilerplate. The party that did not provide the data is the party that operates the system and collects the tax, and in the same period it was the party asking the states to accept its own arithmetic on compensation shortfalls computed from that same data.
differentFactsNote: The certificate says what it says and nobody disputes it. The disagreement is whether non-provision of a national dataset to a state audit is a confidentiality constraint or a refusal, which is a weighting of one agreed record.

unmeasured.why: The requester is named — the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, a constitutional office under Articles 148-151. The non-provision is recorded by the requester itself, in the audit certificate on which a state's accounts stand, and dated by the certificate for the year ended 31 March 2019. What is NOT established is the date of the request itself, its addressee, and whether access was subsequently granted; the grade rests on the date of the recorded refusal rather than of the request, and that limit is stated on the record rather than hidden by it.

title: Bihar enlarged its Contingency Fund twenty-seven-fold and used it to meet its own share of centrally sponsored schemes
summary: Bihar's Contingency Fund corpus was enlarged from ₹350 crore to ₹9,500 crore. The Comptroller and Auditor General found 116 withdrawals totalling ₹6,395.47 crore in FY2022-23, of which 15 withdrawals totalling ₹3,327.42 crore — 52 per cent of the amount — were for expenditure that was foreseeable and should have been budgeted. In the same year the State did not transfer ₹2,258.37 crore of its own share of centrally sponsored schemes to the Single Nodal Accounts, and the transfer lag on shared schemes ran to 181 days. Bihar's own tax revenue is 22 to 25 per cent of its revenue receipts and 5.6 per cent of its state domestic product; its reliance on devolution and grants is 72.3 per cent of revenue receipts against an all-states 42.2.
assessmentNote: Contested rather than failed. The Union's design intent — that states co-own schemes so that they choose them well — and the auditor's finding — that the state could not budget its share and used a constitutional emergency instrument for a foreseeable recurring liability — are both defensible on the same facts, and no retrieved instrument adjudicates between them.
caseFor: This is the case for conditionality, stated on the recipient side. A state that receives 72.3 per cent of its revenue receipts from the Union and raises 5.6 per cent of its state product in its own taxes is the reason matching shares exist: a scheme wholly funded by the Union in a state with no fiscal stake in it will be chosen for the money rather than for the need. Bihar is also the largest per-capita beneficiary of the horizontal formula, at 1.15 times its population share against Tamil Nadu's 0.67, so the transfer system is doing precisely what its designers intended. The Contingency Fund enlargement is a decision of the State legislature within its own competence, and using it to keep central schemes running is a state prioritising delivery over accounting form.
caseAgainst: A Contingency Fund exists for unforeseen expenditure and the auditor found that a majority of the money drawn from it was foreseeable. A matching share on a recurring scheme is the most foreseeable liability a state has, and a state that must reach for an emergency instrument to pay it is telling the Union something about the design of the ratio, not about its own diligence. The lag then compounds: ₹2,258.37 crore of state share not transferred and 181 days of delay mean the central money sits in a nodal account unusable, so the conditionality intended to buy accountability produces idle balances instead. And the state's low own-tax base is not evidence against the argument but the premise of it: a ratio calibrated to the median state is a different instrument in the poorest one.
differentFactsNote: Every figure is the auditor's, drawn from the state's own Finance Accounts and from the Union's payment system, and neither government disputes them. The disagreement is about what a matching share does in a state with Bihar's own-revenue base, which is a weighting of one ledger.

title: Released, received, passed on: three numbers for the same money, and only the auditor computes the difference
summary: For centrally sponsored schemes in Bihar in FY2022-23 the Comptroller and Auditor General sets three figures for one flow of money side by side: ₹24,398.36 crore released by the Union according to its own payment system, ₹22,481.46 crore received in the State treasury, and ₹22,231.91 crore reaching the implementing agencies. In Tamil Nadu the same instrument shows the Union's system reporting ₹14,137.90 crore of central share received in FY2022-23 against ₹13,629.21 crore transferred on by the State, with ₹11,453.81 crore unspent in nodal accounts at 31 March 2023, and the note that "the details of the vouchers with respect to expenditure are not available in the AG (A&E) office". "Released" is not "received" and is not "passed on", and no bridging instrument between the three is published by either government.
assessmentNote: No objective was stated at announcement: the three quantities are accounting facts, not a measure with a claimed outcome. The finding — that the Union's release figure, the state's receipt figure and the agency's figure are three different numbers with no published bridge — is firmly established from two states' audit reports and is the most reusable result in this phase.
caseFor: The three figures are not inconsistent; they are three events on a payment chain that necessarily take time, and the differences are small — under 8 per cent between the outer two in Bihar. Every one of them is published: the Union's release figure in its own payment system, the receipt in the state's Finance Accounts, the onward transfer in the nodal account. The state, not the Union, controls two of the three legs, and the Union has spent five years tightening exactly this chain — the Single Nodal Agency model, a 21-day transfer deadline, penal interest on delay and a validation check that blocks release when the nodal balance is too high — precisely so that money does not sit idle between the legs.
caseAgainst: When a state says it did not receive what the Union says it released, both can be telling the truth, and no published instrument settles which leg the difference sits in. That is the structural reason the whole Centre-state transfer argument is unresolvable in public: the parties are not lying to each other, they are counting different events, and neither publishes the bridge. The consequence in Tamil Nadu is sharper still — the accountant general's office does not hold the vouchers for expenditure from money that passed through a Union-run system into a state-run account. And the tightening the Union cites is itself the withholding mechanism: there is no clause anywhere reading "the Union may withhold", because a tranche simply does not move unless the payment system validates the conditions.
differentFactsNote: The three figures come from one auditor reading both governments' records and neither government disputes them. What is disputed is whether an unbridged three-way difference is ordinary payment latency or a structural failure of accountability, which is a weighting of one agreed record.

unmeasured.what: A bridging statement reconciling funds released by the Union, funds received in a state treasury and funds reaching implementing agencies
unmeasured.why: Neither government publishes one. The Union publishes releases, the state's Finance Accounts publish receipts, and the difference exists only where an auditor performs the subtraction — which it does state by state, in reports published at different times on different templates, and never nationally.

title: Asked what cesses and surcharges come to, the Union gives Parliament a third answer, and defines the quantity in neither of the two it has given
summary: The share of gross tax revenue taken by cesses and surcharges is the central number in the Centre-state fiscal argument, and no statute defines the set it sums. Asked directly, in both Houses in July 2026, the Ministry of Finance laid a table on the Table of the House giving cesses at 11.5, 10.5, 10.0, 8.2 and 6.2 per cent of gross tax revenue for FY2022-23 to BE2026-27 and surcharges at 8.9, 8.0, 7.9, 8.2 and 8.1 per cent, and on the longer span 9.6 per cent for FY2014-15 against 17.9 for FY2024-25. This is a third convention, differing from both cess series already in this drop, and the answer nowhere states what a levy must be to belong to either aggregate.
whatHappened: Two answers three years apart cannot both describe the same set. On 1 August 2023 the Department of Economic Affairs put surcharge at 1.50 per cent of gross tax revenue for FY2021-22; on 21 July 2026 the Department of Revenue put it at 8.9 per cent for FY2022-23. The difference is visible in the later table's own rows and stated in neither answer: the 2026 aggregate counts the Special Additional Excise Duty on petrol and diesel, at 147,163.79 crore fifty-four per cent of its own surcharge total, and the Social Welfare Surcharge on customs; the 2023 aggregate cannot accommodate them at its magnitude. The 2026 answer is at least internally consistent — its cess and surcharge footings sum exactly to the combined figures given in the Lok Sabha the day before. A third form again appears on 4 August 2026, in rupees rather than shares: 32.05 lakh crore of cesses and surcharges over five years, of which 18.88 lakh crore is cesses, leaving about 13.17 lakh crore of surcharge, with the Union stating in terms that "only cesses are collected for designated purposes". The same answers carry the Union's constitutional position verbatim and unchanged across five and a half months: Article 270(1) "exempts cesses and surcharges from distribution between the Union and the States and hence do not form part of the divisible pool".
assessmentNote: No objective was stated for the aggregate. The Union was asked for a figure and gave one; it did not undertake to define the set, and nothing in the answer claims a definition. What the record finds is that the defining body's own statements are two, not one, and that neither is defined — which is a finding about the instrument, not a failure against a claim.
caseFor: Each answer is responsive, accurate on its own rows and laid on the record with the components printed, so any reader can add the seventeen cess lines and the five surcharge lines and get the footing. The two answers came from two different departments, five days short of three years apart, to two differently worded questions, and neither claimed to be continuing the other's series. The underlying collections are not in dispute anywhere: every figure in every version restates the same Department of Revenue receipts, and the Union publishes the line items so the reader can select their own set. And the constitutional position the answers give is correct and has never been contested: Article 270(1) does exempt cesses and Article 271 surcharges, and no Commission or court has said otherwise.
caseAgainst: The figure governs the argument, and the party that collects the money is also the only party that states the figure — twice, differently, and without saying what either version contains. A reader told by the Finance Minister that surcharge is 8.9 per cent of gross tax revenue and by a Minister of State that it is 1.50 per cent has been given the same underlying money on two conventions and cannot tell which, because neither answer names its test for membership. That is not an occasional lapse: the questions asked in both Houses were specifically for the share, and the share is precisely the thing a definition is needed for. The Union also answered a question about the proportion of DIRECT TAX collections with the proportion of gross tax revenue instead, and the substitution passes without remark in the same document.
differentFactsNote: Both sides accept every rupee figure printed in both answers; the disagreement is whether an aggregate stated without a membership test is a measurement or a presentation. That is a weighting of one agreed record, not two ledgers — which is exactly why the spread contains no evidentiary disagreement anywhere.

unmeasured.why: Neither answer states one. The 2026 answer enumerates seventeen cess rows and five surcharge rows and prints a footing percentage; the 2023 answer prints two rows and two percentages with no enumeration at all. Article 270(1), which creates the category, supplies no list and no test, and the Receipt Budget carries no total line for either aggregate.

title: The Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Fund received nothing in the cess's first two full years, and the Union's own table strikes the balance
summary: A cess sits outside the divisible pool because it is levied for a stated purpose. The Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess was levied by the Finance Act 2021 to finance agricultural infrastructure through a named Fund. Answering the Rajya Sabha on 3 February 2026, the Ministry of Finance printed collection, transfer and balance for that Fund in one table: 76,950.68 crore collected in FY2021-22 and 74,142.03 crore in FY2022-23, with the transfer column empty in both years and the whole of the collection carried into the balance column. The first transfer, 120,714.39 crore, came in FY2023-24.
whatHappened: The Union's own arithmetic fixes the two nil years: it subtracts the transfer column from the collection column and prints a balance equal to the entire collection, so the transfer is zero and not merely unreported. A second and unrelated answer, laid in the Lok Sabha on 20 July 2026, prints an ellipsis against the same Fund for FY2022-23 in a column carrying figures for six other funds. From FY2023-24 the direction reverses and transfers exceed each year's collection — 1.49 times in FY2023-24 — as the Fund catches up. It does not catch up within the table: across the five years the Union states collections of 387,226.31 crore against transfers of 377,213.61 crore, so on Budget Estimates the Fund is still 10,012.70 crore behind cumulatively. The year-by-year balance column the Union prints turns negative from FY2023-24 and reads as over-transfer; the cumulative position does not, and both figures are arithmetic from the same five rows. The answer states in terms where the money sat: proceeds "are collected and deposited in Consolidated Fund of India in terms of Articles 266".
assessmentNote: Partly, against the earmark that is the levy's own justification for sitting outside the divisible pool: the Fund received nothing for two years and then received more than each year's collection for three, so the earmark was honoured late and, cumulatively across the published table, not yet in full. The value scores the transfer to the designated Fund and nothing else. It does not score whether agricultural infrastructure was financed, which is a different question answered from the Consolidated Fund under appropriation.
caseFor: Money in the Consolidated Fund is not money lost. Expenditure on agricultural infrastructure is made under parliamentary appropriation whether or not a reserve fund has been constituted, and a fund created before the expenditure programme exists parks money rather than deploying it. The Union has since transferred more than it collected in three successive years, which is what catching up looks like, and it publishes collection, transfer and balance for every cess in one table so the arithmetic can be done by anyone. The transfers are also large in absolute terms: 377,213.61 crore over five years against 387,226.31 crore collected is 97.4 per cent, which on the same table is a better record than several funds that received nothing at all across the whole period.
caseAgainst: The constitutional exemption is not free. Article 270(1) removes a cess from the divisible pool because it is levied for a specific purpose, and for two years the purpose received nothing while 151,092.71 crore accumulated. During those two years the levy was neither shared with the states nor applied to the fund that exempted it from sharing, and the states had no claim on either leg. The Union's own presentation makes this harder to see rather than easier: the balance column resets each year, so from FY2023-24 the table shows a run of negative balances that read as generosity, and the cumulative shortfall of 10,012.70 crore appears nowhere. And the transfer column mixes transfer with utilisation, so even the years that look complete cannot be decomposed from within the document.
differentFactsNote: Every figure on both sides is the Union's own and neither side disputes any of them. The disagreement is whether the earmark is a promise about a fund or a promise about spending — a weighting of one agreed table.

unmeasured.why: The Union prints them as a single column headed "(Transfer/Utilisation)" and states no split. A year showing 120,714.39 crore cannot be decomposed into money credited and money spent from within the document, so the Fund's actual balance at any date is not derivable from the published table.

title: A cess levied since 1974 had no Reserve Fund to be credited to until FY2024-25, and the Union says so in a footnote
summary: In the same annexure that shows the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Fund receiving nothing for two years, the Union shows the Oil Industry Development Fund receiving nothing for four: FY2020-21, FY2021-22, FY2022-23 and FY2023-24, against collections of 11,474.15, 19,324.29, 21,629.22 and 18,803.41 crore under the cess on crude oil. The reason is in the answer's own footnote, and it is not an accounting lag: "The Reserve Fund in the Public Account of India has, however, been operationalized, going forward, from FY 2024-25." The cess is levied under the Oil Industry (Development) Act 1974.
whatHappened: Four consecutive nil years total 71,231.07 crore collected under an earmarked levy with no fund in the Public Account for it to be credited to. From FY2024-25 the fund exists and the transfer tracks the collection closely — 17,730.00 crore against 17,810.00 collected on Revised Estimates, and 19,376.03 against 19,330.00 on Budget Estimates. The footnote is the concession: the absence of transfer was not a failure to move money between two accounts but the absence of the second account. The same table shows the same shape a second time in the same document, at the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Fund, where the CAG recorded "Fund not created as yet" for FY2022-23; and the Union separately told Parliament that the three Health and Education Cess funds were operationalised only from FY2022-23, after obtaining the approval of the Comptroller and Auditor General in December 2022. The Union's own aggregate across all cesses and surcharges — 21.38 lakh crore transferred against 18.88 lakh crore of cess collections over five years — is net of these two funds, and conceals both.
assessmentNote: The value records what this drop holds, not a judgement that no objective existed. The Oil Industry (Development) Act 1974 names the Fund and was NOT retrieved in this run, so the statutory objective against which the fifty-year absence would be scored is not in evidence here. Re-score if the Act is obtained: on its face this is a candidate for failed, and the record should not be read as saying otherwise.
caseFor: The cess was collected, accounted for in the Consolidated Fund and appropriated by Parliament throughout; nothing was unaccounted and nothing was outside audit. The oil development expenditure the levy funds was made from the Consolidated Fund on parliamentary appropriation in every one of those years, and a reserve fund in the Public Account is an accounting device for earmarking, not a precondition for spending. The Union has now constituted the fund and discloses the whole sequence, including the four nil years, in a table it was not obliged to lay in that form. And it disclosed the reason in its own footnote rather than leaving the nil years to be explained by others.
caseAgainst: A levy is exempt from sharing with the states because it is earmarked, and for four of the years in this table — on the Union's own footnote, for fifty years — there was no instrument in which the earmark could be recorded. The claim that a cess is different in kind from a tax rests on the fund; where the fund does not exist the difference is a statement of intent and nothing more. The disclosure also comes only in answer to a question: the fund's non-existence is stated in a footnote to an annexure, not in the Receipt Budget that reports the collection every year.
differentFactsNote: The collections, the four nil years and the operationalisation date are all the Union's own and are not disputed. What is disputed is whether an earmark with no fund behind it is a defect or a formality — a weighting of one agreed record.

unmeasured.what: Where the cess on crude oil was applied in the four years in which no Reserve Fund existed
unmeasured.why: The Union's table has a transfer column and a balance column and no application column. With no fund in the Public Account there is no instrument that records the earmarked money separately from general Consolidated Fund expenditure, so the question cannot be answered from any published account.

unmeasured.wouldFill: The Oil Industry (Development) Act 1974 as published on India Code.

title: Centrally sponsored scheme releases to West Bengal fell 67 per cent in five years while the national total fell 6, and the Union states four general conditions and no state-specific reason
summary: Answering the Lok Sabha on 1 December 2025 from the Public Financial Management System, the Department of Expenditure published centrally sponsored scheme releases by state for FY2020-21 to FY2024-25. West Bengal falls from 27,406.79 to 9,081.21 crore, a fall of 66.9 per cent, monotonic in every one of the four transitions with no reversal. Over the same five years the all-India total falls 5.8 per cent, Bihar rises 21.4 per cent and Tamil Nadu falls 10.9 per cent from a peak in the fourth year. West Bengal goes from the second-largest recipient in the table to smaller than Punjab, Himachal Pradesh or Tripura.
whatHappened: As a share of the all-India total West Bengal falls from 7.10 to 2.50 per cent. The question asked whether the Government was aware that delayed release had adversely affected states; the reply neither confirms nor denies, and instead restates the release conditions in full: funds are released "as per the scheme guidelines, demand from State, submission of Utilization Certificates of the funds released earlier and contribution of commensurate State Share". Those four conditions are the Union's stated levers. The answer names them without saying which, if any, applied to any state, and offers no explanation for any state's trajectory. The same answer's second annexure cuts the other way and must be carried with the first: West Bengal's CENTRAL SECTOR scheme releases ROSE 57.5 per cent over the identical five years, from 15,898.10 to 25,035.43 crore. That annexure also contains an artefact that disqualifies it as a geography: Delhi appears at 5.56 lakh crore in FY2024-25, 59 per cent of the national Central Sector total, because releases to central ministries and implementing agencies headquartered in Delhi are booked against Delhi, and the document's own footnote warns that "The figures include release to State Treasury as well as Implementing Agencies."
assessmentNote: Contested rather than failed: the same table supports a reading of conditions unmet and a reading of a state squeezed, and no instrument in the record adjudicates between them. What would settle it — a statement of which condition was unmet, by which state, in which year, on which scheme — is not published by anyone, and the answer that was asked for it gave the conditions in the abstract instead.
caseFor: Centrally sponsored schemes are conditional transfers by design and the conditions are published, uniform and old: guidelines, demand, utilisation certificates for money already released, and a matching state share. A state that does not demand, does not certify, or does not match receives less, and that is the scheme working rather than failing. The Union releases to twenty-eight states on one system and publishes the whole table, including the rows that embarrass it. On the same table Bihar rose and Tamil Nadu peaked in the fourth year, so no national squeeze is visible. And the second annexure of the same answer shows West Bengal's Central Sector releases rising by more than half over the same period — money going to the same state through a different channel, which is difficult to reconcile with a policy of squeezing a state.
caseAgainst: The fall is monotonic across four transitions, which no ordinary conditionality produces: utilisation certificates and matching shares vary year to year, and a state that failed them would recover in some year. It did not, in any year. The Union holds the reason — it decides each release against four conditions it names — and when asked in Parliament whether delay had harmed states, answered with the conditions rather than with the facts of any state. The largest single component of the decline is MGNREGA, where a statutory power to stop release was exercised against this state and no other, and restored by a court rather than by the Ministry. And the Central Sector rise is not an answer: those releases go substantially to implementing agencies rather than to the state government, on the same document's own footnote, so the two annexures do not measure the same relationship.
differentFactsNote: Both sides read the same two annexures of the same answer and neither disputes a figure in either. The disagreement is about which annexure measures the relationship in question and about what a monotonic decline implies in the absence of a stated reason — a weighting of one agreed record.

title: Samagra Shiksha: two states received nil, one had it paid back in arrears and one did not, and the only state-specific reason the Union gives is an unsigned memorandum for a different scheme
summary: Answering the Lok Sabha on 30 March 2026, the Department of School Education and Literacy published central allocation against central share released under Samagra Shiksha, by state, for five years. West Bengal was paid 97.8 per cent of allocation in FY2021-22 and 85.8 per cent in FY2022-23, then 17.6 per cent in FY2023-24, then nil in FY2024-25 and nil again in FY2025-26 — 3,744.19 crore allocated across the two nil years and nothing released. Tamil Nadu was also nil in FY2024-25. Bihar, on the same table in the same years, was paid between 70.8 and 93.8 per cent throughout.
whatHappened: The asymmetry is the finding and it is in the Union's own footnote. Tamil Nadu's FY2025-26 release of 626.20 crore is marked as including 362.81 crore "for FY 2024-25" — so Tamil Nadu's zero was part-paid in arrears, at 16.9 per cent of the allocation it had lost. No such note appears against West Bengal, which has received nothing for either year. A delay and a stoppage look identical in a single-year view and are distinguished here only because the table runs five years and carries the asterisk. The zeros are also not a national shortfall: the all-India total released stayed between 29,996.83 and 34,458.21 crore across all five years, and Bihar was paid 93.8 per cent in the same year West Bengal received nil. Asked directly whether funds had been withheld from states not implementing PM SHRI, the reply does not say yes and does not say no, and then supplies the linkage itself: states "are required to sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)... for implementation of PM SHRI scheme. However, West Bengal has not signed the PM SHRI MoU", followed by "repeated reminders at the level of Secretary and Union Minister". The two schemes are legally distinct. The answer offers no other state-specific reason for any state, and closes the distinction outright: "implementation of Samagra Shiksha Scheme is implementation of NEP 2020 and PM SHRI Schools are exemplar schools of NEP 2020." The general conditions it also cites are the Ministry of Finance ones — pace of expenditure, receipt of commensurate state share, audited accounts, outstanding advances, expenditure statements.
assessmentNote: Contested: the record supports a reading in which release conditions were unmet and a reading in which participation in a separate scheme was made a condition of funding an existing one, and the answer that would choose between them declines to. The Union does not say the funds were stopped for the MoU; it says the MoU is unsigned, in reply to a question about why the funds were not released, and gives nothing else state-specific.
caseFor: Samagra Shiksha is a shared scheme with published release conditions set by the Ministry of Finance, and they are the same conditions for every state: pace of expenditure, commensurate state share, audited accounts, statements of outstanding advances. Bihar met them and was paid; Tamil Nadu's shortfall was made good in arrears, which shows the process is a payment cycle rather than a bar. Education is on the Concurrent List, the answer says so at the outset, and a Union that funds a scheme may condition its money on the scheme being implemented as designed. The Government also states that it followed up the outstanding memorandum with requests and reminders at Secretary and Ministerial level and received no response, which is a description of a stalled administrative process rather than a sanction.
caseAgainst: Asked for the reasons for not releasing money under one scheme, the Government answered with the non-signature of a memorandum under another, and named nothing else specific to the state. The two schemes are separate in law and separately funded, and the answer's own closing sentence collapses them. The allocation continued through both nil years and rose 14.5 per cent in the second, so the Union did not treat West Bengal as ineligible; it allocated and did not release. And the arrears asterisk is the control: the same Government, in the same table, records a payment made late to one state and records nothing for the other, so the difference between the two zeros is on the face of the document. What is at stake is not a scheme's budget but a statutory entitlement to schooling in a state of ninety million people, and the answer supplies no test by which the release could be regained.
differentFactsNote: Both sides read the same annexure and the same reply and dispute no figure and no quotation in either. The disagreement is whether an unsigned memorandum for a second scheme, offered as the only state-specific fact in a reply about the first, is an explanation or an implication — a weighting of one agreed record.

title: "No additional burden on the consumer" was true of three grades of fuel out of four: branded diesel became one paisa a litre dearer
summary: The February 2021 excise restructuring imposed an Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess and cut basic and special additional excise duty to offset it. The Union stated in four documents that the consumer would bear no additional burden. On the retrieved before-rates and the Union's own after-rates the arithmetic holds for unbranded petrol (minus 8 paise), branded petrol (minus 6 paise) and unbranded diesel (minus 3 paise), and fails for branded diesel: minus 2.99 on basic duty, minus 1.00 on special additional duty and plus 4.00 of cess is plus 0.01. Branded-diesel buyers paid one paisa more a litre from 2 February 2021.
claimAtLaunch: Four formulations, each universal in its terms: the Budget Speech at para 188 ("not to put additional burden on consumers on most items"); the Annexure to Part B at para 5, on petrol and diesel specifically ("so that overall consumer does not bear any additional burden"); the Memorandum's section V ("so that consumer does not have to bear any additional burden on account of imposition of AIDC"); and the Tax Research Unit covering letter ("calibrated so that there would be no additional burden on the consumer").
whatHappened: The four grades, in rupees per litre. Unbranded petrol: basic duty 2.98 to 1.40, special additional 12 to 11, cess plus 2.50, road cess unchanged at 18, total 32.98 to 32.90. Branded petrol: 4.16 to 2.60, 12 to 11, plus 2.50, total 34.16 to 34.10. Unbranded diesel: 4.83 to 1.80, 9 to 8, plus 4.00, total 31.83 to 31.80. Branded diesel: 7.19 to 4.20, 9 to 8, plus 4.00, total 34.19 to 34.20. The leg-sum identity holds on all four grades, so the table is internally consistent as well as consistent with the government's own after-totals. The magnitude of the failure is trivial and the universality of the claim is not: three of the four statements are unqualified, and the fourth qualifies with "most items" in a paragraph that does not name fuel at all. The before rates are not in any 2021-22 budget document — verified against a positive control — and had to be retrieved from the amending notifications the 2021 notifications themselves name and from the Petroleum Ministry's tariff table, which agree on all four basic-duty rates and both special-additional rates.
assessmentNote: Partly, and narrowly: the stated objective was met on three grades of four and missed on the fourth by one paisa. The value scores the consumer-neutrality claim alone. The effect on the divisible pool is scored at L-0157 and is not re-scored here.
caseFor: One paisa on the least-sold of four grades is not a burden in any sense a consumer could detect, and the calibration achieved on the other three — eight, six and three paise, all downward — is remarkably fine work for a package assembled in a budget cycle. Branded diesel carries a higher basic duty precisely because it is a premium product, and the cut applied to it, 2.99, was the largest of the four in absolute terms; the residual arises because the cess is a flat 4.00 across both diesel grades while the offsetting cuts are not. Nothing in the record suggests the outcome was sought, and the Budget Speech's own formulation is qualified: "most items".
caseAgainst: Three of the four statements are unqualified and one of them is specific to petrol and diesel. A claim stated four times in four documents, in terms that admit no exception, was false of one of the four things it was about, and the Union had every rate in front of it when it made the claim. The reader could not check it: no 2021-22 budget document prints the rates in force before 2 February 2021, so the assertion was made in prose and never demonstrated in a table — unlike the identical operation in 2018, whose annexure printed both a From and a To column and can be verified in place. And the single arithmetic error in the government's own summary table falls on exactly this row, which is recorded separately at L-0181.
differentFactsNote: The rates, the totals and the claim are all the Union's own or come from its own notifications, and no figure is disputed. The disagreement is whether a universal claim that fails by one paisa on one grade is a failure or a rounding of language — a weighting of one agreed arithmetic.

unmeasured.why: Verified absent against a positive control: the post-change rate 1.40 returns hits in exactly the two documents in which it was read, and the composite total 32.90 in one, so the search works; the pre-change rates 2.98, 4.83 and a decoy 6.48 return zero substantive hits across the Budget Speech, the Finance Bill, the Memorandum, the Tax Research Unit letter and both notifications. Every 2021-22 document states only the revised structure. The Union holds the before rates — it set them by notification — and did not print them beside the claim they were needed to test.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A budget annexure printing the From column alongside the To column, as the Budget Speech 2018-19 annexure did for the identical operation three years earlier.

title: The one arithmetic error in the Union's own summary table is on the one row where the consumer's burden rose
summary: The Tax Research Unit's covering letter of 1 February 2021 summarised the excise restructuring in a four-row table of components and totals. Three rows add up. The fourth, branded diesel, prints components of 4.20, 8, 18 and 4.0 and a total of 34.10; those components sum to 34.20. The error is ten paise, on one cell, and its effect is that a reader taking the printed total at face value computes a nine-paise reduction for branded diesel and never sees the one-paisa increase that the correct total shows.
whatHappened: The mismatch is not a text-extraction artefact: the source page was rendered to an image at 150 dots per inch and read visually, and the row unambiguously prints 34.10. The component figure is the reliable one and the total is the wrong one — branded diesel's basic excise duty of 4.20 is independently confirmed twice, by the Memorandum's own section V table and by notification 01/2021-Central Excise. The likeliest mechanical explanation is on the face of the table: the row directly above, branded petrol, carries 34.10 correctly, and a copy-down produces exactly this error. Two further defects in the same package were found in the same pass and are recorded here because each is a live trap rather than a curiosity. Notification 01/2021-Central Excise misdescribes its own principal notification's amendment history, citing "No. 19/2018-Central Excise dated 31st December, 2019" — a 2018 number against a 2019 date; the real 31 December 2019 amendment is 9/2019-Central Excise, which changes tariff codes only, and an archive index query confirmed that 18/2019-CE and 19/2019-CE do not exist, against a positive control returning rows for every other notification in the chain. And a figure carried by a prior pass of this instrument is refuted: branded petrol's basic excise duty before the change was 4.16 a litre, not 4.18, on the amending notification verbatim and on the Petroleum Ministry's tariff table independently.
assessmentNote: No objective was stated for the table's arithmetic, so there is nothing to score it against. The value asserts nothing about the finding's quality: the error is established to a rendered image and the component figures are corroborated twice over.
caseFor: It is one incorrect cell in one summary table in a covering letter, and the letter is not the operative instrument: the rates that bind are in the notifications and the Finance Bill Seventh Schedule, and every one of those is correct. Three of the four rows are right, the components on the wrong row are right, and the error is of a shape — a total carried down from the row above — that occurs in hand-assembled tables everywhere. Nothing turned on it: no duty was collected at the printed total, and the correct rates were in force from 2 February 2021 regardless of what the summary said.
caseAgainst: The letter is the document the trade and the press read on budget day, and its Annexure C is the only place in the entire 2021-22 budget set where the four grades appear with their totals. Its two load-bearing figures, 32.90 and 31.80, are quoted everywhere; a reader who checks them will find the neighbouring row failing and has no basis for deciding which cells to trust. And the error is not neutral in its effect: the single wrong cell is on the single row where the government's own repeated claim of no additional burden does not hold, and it conceals that failure. The two adjacent defects compound the point — a notification that misdescribes its own amendment history sends anyone tracing the before rates to a notification of the wrong year that does not touch them.
differentFactsNote: There is no dispute of fact at all: the components, the printed total and the correct sum are all readable from one rendered page. The disagreement, such as it is, is about how much weight a clerical error in a summary document should carry, which is a weighting of one agreed record.

title: Two Union-origin instruments disagree by ₹67,819 crore about what the states were paid in FY2017-18, and nothing explains it
summary: Tax devolution for FY2017-18 is 605,186 crore in the Sixteenth Finance Commission's Annexure 7.1 and 673,005.29 crore in the Union's own Receipt Budget for the same year. The difference is 67,819.29 crore, 11.2 per cent, and it is 4.6 times the largest divergence between the same two instruments in any other year. FY2017-18 is the year the goods and services tax began. No published document reconciles the two figures and this record does not guess at the component.
whatHappened: The two instruments overlap in eleven years and agree within 240 crore in six of them. Of the four that disagree, three — FY2018-19 by 14,560.15 crore, FY2021-22 by 15,292 and FY2022-23 by 576.18 — are the definitional gap between cash attributed to a year and cash accounted in a year, already documented in this drop from the Commission's own two tables. FY2017-18 is a different order of magnitude and sits outside that explanation. Its arithmetic is exact: 673,005.29 minus 605,186 is 67,819.29 with no residual, which is the signature of one identifiable component being present in one instrument and absent from the other rather than of two vintages of the same aggregate. FY2017-18 is also the year in which Integrated GST first had to be apportioned between the Union and the states, and in which nine months of a new tax replaced eight central levies. That is a place to look and is not a finding: this record states the divergence, states that it is unexplained, and names no component.
assessmentNote: No objective was stated by anyone about the agreement of these two instruments; neither publisher acknowledges the other. What the record finds is a disagreement of a size that changes the answer to an ordinary question, with no published reconciliation.
caseFor: Both figures are correctly sourced and each is right on its own definition, which is the ordinary condition of a federation with two accounting systems. The Commission compiles cash transferred; the Union accounts for what left its books under one major head; the two have never claimed to be the same series and no reader is told they are. Six of eleven years agree to within a rounding error, which is what one would expect of two honest instruments measuring adjacent events. And FY2017-18 was a year of unprecedented accounting disruption in which eight central levies were replaced mid-year — a large one-off difference in that year is the least surprising place for one to appear.
caseAgainst: The number is what twenty-eight states were paid, and two arms of the same government give it differently by an amount larger than the annual devolution of most states. The divergence is not disclosed by either publisher: the Commission does not note that its Annexure differs from the Receipt Budget, and the Receipt Budget does not note that it differs from the Commission. A reader quoting either figure is quoting a correct source and may be 11 per cent wrong for the purpose in hand, with nothing on either page to warn them. The exactness of the residual makes it worse rather than better: an unexplained round difference means a component is being included by one and excluded by the other, which is a definitional fact somebody knows and nobody has written down.
differentFactsNote: Neither side disputes either figure or the arithmetic between them. The disagreement is about whether an undisclosed 11 per cent difference between two official instruments is a normal consequence of different definitions or a defect in publication — a weighting of one agreed record.

unmeasured.what: The component that accounts for the ₹67,819.29 crore difference in FY2017-18
unmeasured.why: Neither publisher acknowledges the other's figure, so neither reconciles to it. The Finance Commission states its own source for Annexure 7.1 and the Receipt Budget states its major head, and no document in either family bridges the two. Candidate components exist — Integrated GST apportionment and prior-period adjustment are the obvious ones in a GST transition year — and this drop names none of them, because a plausible candidate offered without evidence would harden into an explanation.
unmeasured.wouldFill: A Finance Commission or Ministry of Finance note reconciling Annexure 7.1 to the Receipt Budget major head 0710 Actuals for FY2017-18, or a CAG Union Government Finance Accounts paragraph doing the same.
